blocks.h: HOLD ME UP TILL THE HORN
Roya Publication No. 57
by Chew Z
SYNOPSIS

On a Saturday night in September 1932, in a dance hall just outside the Detroit city line, ninety-one couples take the floor for a contest with one rule: keep moving. Forty-five minutes of dancing, fifteen minutes on a cot, around the clock, for as long as a body will hold. Last couple standing takes the prize. If one goes down, both are out.

Alma Sutter enters alone and is paired with a stranger — a Persian man the announcer decides to call Barney, because Bahram is more trouble than it’s worth. She has buried a daughter six weeks ago. He needs the money and won’t say why. Neither of them can afford to be the one who falls.

To keep her awake, he starts telling her a story. It is a thousand years old and it is the only thing he brought with him from home: kings who lose everything, a baby left on a mountain and raised by a bird, a father and a son who meet in single combat without knowing each other’s faces. He can’t stop moving to tell it, so he teaches it to her as steps.

Outside the hall, a country is coming apart and deciding what to do about it. Inside, two thousand people pay a quarter a night to watch the poor come apart on schedule. Doyle Ferrin, who owns the microphone, knows a good story when he sees one — and he knows something about Alma that she has not told anyone.
Eleven hundred hours is forty-six days. They are going to be on that floor for all of it.
A NOTE FROM THE AUTHOR

The thing that started this book was a number. Between 1920 and 1930, two hundred and eight people came to the United States from Persia. Not two hundred thousand. Two hundred and eight, in ten years.

Think about what that means for one of them. No neighbourhood. No restaurant that makes the food you grew up on. Nobody in the state who can say your name, and no one to talk to in your own language, possibly ever again.

Then the Depression comes. A quarter of the country is out of work and people start counting who belongs. Nobody had to pass a law. When there are ten men for one job, the foreign one goes last. So he takes work nobody else wants — which is how a man ends up shuffling in circles for forty-six days in front of a paying crowd, while an announcer calls him a name that isn’t his because the real one is too much bother.

I gave him the only thing he could carry across an ocean for free, which is a story. The Shahnameh is a thousand years old and it is full of people who don’t recognise each other until it is too late. A father fights a stranger, kills him, and finds out afterward it was his son. I have never known whether that is about fate or about something smaller — how easy it is not to say who you are, and how long you can go on not saying it.
I did not have to make the dance marathons worse than they were, and because the whole book sits inside one, it is worth saying plainly what they were.

They began in the 1920s as a stunt for the newspapers — college students setting endurance records. Then the money went out of the world, and by 1932 there were promoters running them in forty states and the people entering were not students. Forty-five minutes on the floor, fifteen off, around the clock. If your knees touched you were out, and if your partner’s knees touched you were out. Contests ran for weeks; the longest on record went past five months.

Detroit is where I put it because Detroit is where the fall was steepest, and the figures Bahram gives on the floor are the real ones. On the seventh of March 1932, three thousand unemployed men walked to the Ford plant at the Rouge to ask for work, and were met with fire hoses in twenty-degree weather and then with gunfire, and four of them were killed. That happened seven months before this book opens, and the man in the third row on the north side was there.

Men did die on marathon floors, and the band did keep playing. Promoters fed their dancers twelve times a day and made sure the newspapers knew it, because a hungry contestant quits. They ran derbies when the gate fell off — races designed to break somebody in front of the house. They held weddings on the floor for money. They ran silver showers, in which a dancer took a microphone and told the crowd the worst thing that had ever happened to them while the audience threw coins. And they put a paid professional or two into the contest, to keep the floor from emptying in the first ten days.
None of that is invention. What is invented is everybody in this book.

The part I keep coming back to is not the cruelty, because it was not really cruelty — nobody in that building was a villain, and the announcer in these pages is the kindest man in it. It is that a country which could not stand to look at its own suffering found it could pay a quarter to watch somebody else’s, on a schedule, with a band.
Chew Z
I. FORTY-FIVE AND FIFTEEN
1. THE PHYSICAL
The sign had been up on Jefferson Avenue for eleven days and Alma had walked past it nine times before she went in.

It was painted on a bedsheet and hung off the front of a building that used to sell Studebakers. Somebody had done the lettering in red and then gone back over it in gold, which meant somebody had cared, and the gold had run in the second line so it looked like the words were bleeding upward.
MARATHON DANCE $1,000 IN CASH THEY GO TILL THEY DROP
Underneath, smaller, in a hand that had gotten tired: Doyle Ferrin Presents.
She went in at four in the afternoon on a Saturday with sixty cents in her coat and the coat buttoned to the throat because the dress under it had been washed too many times to be seen in daylight.

They had taken the cars out and laid a maple floor down over the concrete, and the smell of the varnish was still in the air and made her think, stupidly, of a school. Around three sides they’d built up plank bleachers. Above the stage hung a board the size of a door, blank, with a row of little brass hooks screwed into it — the hour board, she would learn, which was how everybody in that building was going to tell the time for the next six weeks. A boy was up on a ladder screwing in the last of the hooks.
There was a line of maybe forty people at a card table.
“Name.”

The man at the table did not look up. He had a ledger and a fountain pen and a cigarette going in a coffee saucer and he was working fast, the way a man works when he’s been told what he’ll be paid regardless.
“Alma Sutter.”
“Age.”
“Twenty-nine.”
“Partner.”
“I don’t have one.”
Now he looked up. He had a long face and a small mouth and his shirt was clean, which in that room was a kind of shouting.
“You come alone.”
“Yes.”
“Married?”
She said, “My husband’s in Toledo,” which was true, and let him do the rest of it himself, which he did.

“You’ll get matched. You don’t get to pick and you don’t get to trade. Once you’re paired you’re paired till one of you goes down.” He turned the ledger around and put the pen on it. “Read that and sign it.”
She read the first two lines and then read the rest of it the way you read a thing you have already decided to sign.

The undersigned enters of her own free will and holds harmless Ferrin Amusement Co. of Toledo, Ohio, its agents and employees, against injury, illness, collapse, permanent disability, or death arising from participation.
The undersigned agrees that the decision of the judges is final in all matters.
The undersigned certifies that all statements given upon entry are true.
She held the pen a second on that last one.
“Dependents,” the man said. He’d gone back to writing. “Anybody at home. We put it in the program.”
Somebody on the bleachers laughed at something.
“I had a little girl,” Alma said.
The pen stopped.
“Had.”
“July.”
He looked at her then for what felt like a long while and was probably two seconds, and something moved behind the small mouth that she would think about many times later and never be able to name.

“I’m sorry to hear it,” he said, and he was — that was the thing, he really was, she’d have sworn to it — and then he wrote it down, and while he was writing he said, in exactly the same voice, “How old.”
“Four.”
“Name?”
“Ruth.”
He wrote that too. Then he blotted it and turned the ledger back around and said, “Doyle Ferrin,” and put his hand out, and she shook it, and his hand was dry and warm.
“Doc’s in back,” he said. “Through there. Then you’re in.”
It was the twenty-fourth of September, 1932, and what she had just signed is only legible against what that autumn was.

There was no unemployment insurance in Michigan, because there was none anywhere in the country, and the county had run out of money in July and cut the relief rolls in half. A family could be evicted on a Tuesday and be sleeping in Grand Circus Park on the Wednesday with their furniture on the sidewalk, and there were people doing it that week, in numbers.
A great many people were looking for something that paid. There was nothing. So they looked instead for something that fed you, and a dance marathon fed you.

That was the whole of the appeal and it had nothing to do with dancing. You signed a paper, and from that hour a man you had never met gave you twelve meals a day, a cot, a nurse and a roof for as long as you could keep moving, and a thousand dollars at the end if you were the last one standing.
And the people in the bleachers paid a quarter, which was real money, to watch.
The doctor turned her left foot over in his hands like something at a market.

“You got a high arch. That’s good for about three hundred hours. After that it isn’t.” He wrote on his card. “You understand the arch is going to come down. Flatten. Permanently. Most of the girls that go long, it happens.” He said it the way you’d say it looks like rain. “Once it comes down it doesn’t go back up. You’ll walk different the rest of your life.”
Alma looked at her own feet on the cold floor of a parts department, and thought about the rest of her life, and found that it had gotten very short and very simple and had one thing in it.
“How long is three hundred hours,” she said.
“Twelve, thirteen days.”
“And the contest runs?”
The doctor laughed once, without any humor in it at all.
“Lady,” he said, “the last one of these I worked ran forty-one days.”

They put her in a green dress from a rack of forty identical ones, and they would be in every photograph anybody ever took of her. A woman in white with hands like a bricklayer’s pinned the number 63 to her back.

“I’m Ida. I’m the nurse. You’ll see more of me than you’ll see of God.” She worked the second pin through. “Eat everything they put in front of you. Every time. Even when you can’t. Especially when you can’t. And keep your mouth shut about your feet. You go to the doc, he tells Doyle, and Doyle finds a way to make it a thing.”
“A thing.”
“A story, hon,” Ida said. “Everything in here is a story. They pay a quarter for it.”
At half past eight they let the crowd in.

There were, she would read later in the Free Press, nineteen hundred people in that room. It was a Saturday night in the third year of the worst thing that had ever happened to any of them. They had all found a quarter. They had all decided that this was what the quarter was for.

A boy of about fifteen called Sonny — he was Fitz the piano player’s nephew and he was paid two dollars a week to do it — went up the ladder at the back of the stage and hung a single brass numeral on the first hook of the board.

That was the clock. There would be no other. Sonny went up that ladder every hour of every day and night for the next forty-six days and changed the number, and the whole room turned to watch him do it, and a woman in the bleachers would say to her husband, forty-one, and he would say, is that all.
Then Doyle Ferrin came out with a microphone on a cord and the room stood up.

He was good. She hadn’t expected him to be good. He got them laughing in under a minute and he did it without saying anything funny, just by the rhythm of it, and Alma understood that whatever else this was, it was the man’s trade, and he was better at his trade than she had ever been at hers.

“Ninety-one couples,” Doyle said. “Forty-five minutes on. Fifteen minutes off. Around the clock. Cots come out at midnight and you can watch ’em sleep, folks, that’s included in the price of admission and there’s no other show in Michigan where you can say that.”
Laughter.
“Rule number one. You keep moving. Rule number two.” He let it sit. “If one goes down — both go home.”
And the room made a sound Alma had never heard before, a low warm ohhh, nineteen hundred people receiving good news.
They called the unmatched out to the middle of the floor — four women in green and eleven men in shirtsleeves, standing in the light in front of everybody, while Doyle worked the crowd about it.
“Number sixty-three. Mrs. Sutter, come out here.”
She came out.

“And let’s see.” He walked the line of men. He was enjoying it. He put his hand on one and moved on, and on the third he stopped and turned around and grinned at the bleachers with the whole of his face.
“Well now,” he said. “Folks, we got ourselves a prince.”
The man he’d stopped at was maybe thirty. Black hair, a good jaw gone thin, sleeves rolled twice, and he had the stillness of somebody standing in a room he has decided not to be surprised by.
“What’s the name, friend?”
The man said it.
Doyle put the microphone closer. “Say again?”
He said it again.
“Bah— ” Doyle looked at the crowd and the crowd laughed, and he laughed with them, and it was the friendliest sound in the world. “Folks, I can’t get around that one. Where’s that from, friend?”
“Persia.”

“Persia.” Doyle said it the way you’d unwrap something. “Ladies and gentlemen, all the way from Persia. That’s your Arabian Nights, that’s your flying carpets. That’s your sheiks.” He put a hand up against the noise. “Now what do we call you, pal, on account of I got to say it four hundred times.”
The man looked at Doyle for a moment.
“Bahram,” he said.
“Barney,” Doyle said.
The bleachers went up like a struck match.

Alma watched the man’s face while it happened. There was nothing on it. He waited out the noise, and then he put his hand out toward her, palm up, the way you would offer to help somebody down off a step, and he said, under all of it, so quietly that only she could possibly have heard:
“Not one word from that man is going to be true. It will be easier if you know it now.”
She put her hand in his.
At nine o’clock the boy took the numeral off the hook and hung up a 1, and the band started, and ninety-one couples began to move.
2. FORTY-FIVE AND FIFTEEN

The first thing she learned was that nobody danced. What it was, was walking — two people holding each other loosely and going in a slow counterclockwise circle on a maple floor while a band played, and never stopping.

“Don’t lift your feet,” the man said. He had a low voice and a careful way of putting a sentence down, like a man setting a full cup on a table. “Slide them. You will lift them nine thousand times tonight and by tomorrow you will not be able to.”
She tried it. It felt ridiculous, a shuffle, an old woman’s walk.
“How do you know that?”
“I don’t. A man told me at the door.” He turned them a little to take the corner. “He was very sure.”

At forty-five minutes the air horn went off. It was mounted over the stage and it was the loudest thing Alma had ever been in a room with. Ninety-one couples came off the floor in a body, through a gap in the bleachers, into the old parts department where they had set up the cots in two long rows, women’s side and men’s side, with a canvas hung between.
Fifteen minutes.

She lay down in the green dress with her shoes on because a woman on the next cot told her not to take them off — you take ’em off tonight and tomorrow they won’t go back on — and it seemed to her that she had barely got flat before the horn went again.
That was hour one.

By the eighth she understood the shape of the thing. Not the pain; there wasn’t any pain yet, that was the trick of it, that was why ninety-one couples had signed. It was that the fifteen minutes had stopped being a rest and become a thing that was taken away from her, every hour, forever.

At midnight they brought the cots out onto the floor — eight iron beds wheeled under the lights in front of the bleachers, and Doyle explaining warmly that folks, these here are your leaders, and they’re going to take their rest right where you can see ’em. Alma watched a girl of maybe twenty from Wyandotte lie down in the middle of a maple floor and put her forearm over her eyes and go to sleep, actually go to sleep, with nineteen hundred people looking at her.
“They are the lucky ones,” the man said.
“How is that lucky.”

“Because they will not have to walk while they sleep.” He was quiet a moment. “In two weeks you will want that cot very badly. You will want them to put you in the light so you can lie down. You should know that about yourself early. It will save you from being surprised.”

Thirty-one couples went in the first two days. She had thought it would be a slow thinning and instead it was a slaughter, and the kind things were the worst — Doyle never mocked anybody on the way out, he gave them a send-off, he said let’s hear it for a fella that gave us everything he had, and it was so generous, and it made you want so badly to be the one still standing when it was said about somebody else, that Alma understood by the third morning that the kindness was part of the machinery and possibly the most expensive part.

The song came out of nothing on the Wednesday of the first week — the twenty-eighth of September, hour ninety-three, fifty-one couples still upright of the ninety-one who had started. Doyle had written it himself and admitted it freely at the microphone, the way he admitted everything: folks, I wrote this on a train outside Sandusky and it took me nine minutes.
The bank took the farm and the farm took the man,
I got two left shoes and a coffee can,
But the sign said DANCE and I said I can —
So hold me up till the horn.

Every couple that goes out, folks, they get a verse. That’s their verse. It belongs to them now. And the couple going out would be crying with exhaustion and gratitude at the door, and the band would play the new verse, and nineteen hundred people would learn it, and it would be theirs forever.
“He is very good at this,” Bahram said.
“He’s terrible.”

“He is both. Do you know what the song does? It teaches them that going out is beautiful. It is the most useful thing in this building. In two weeks, when you are finished, you will not want to stop. You will want your verse.” He walked her past the bandstand. “You say a thing in front of enough people and it becomes true whether or not anybody has written it down. That is the most dangerous thing I know about this country and I have been trying to explain it to myself for eight years.”
He corrected Doyle once, and only once, and it was on the sixth night.

Doyle had settled into calling him the Sheik — somebody in the bleachers had shouted it and Doyle had taken it the way he took everything, gratefully, and made it his own inside of an evening. There he goes, folks, the Sheik of Ecorse, straight off the flying carpet.

And Bahram stopped, mid-circle, which you were allowed to do so long as you kept your feet going, and said to Doyle, not into the microphone, without heat, the way you would tell a man his shoelace was undone:

“A sheik is an Arab. I am not an Arab. Persia is a different country and a different language and the difference is about as large as the difference between you and a Frenchman. There is also no harem. I worked eleven years at the Rouge.”
Doyle looked at him with real interest.
“That so,” he said.
“That is so.”
“Huh,” Doyle said, and nodded slowly, and turned away with the microphone still live and said, “Ladies and gentlemen — the Sheik of Ecorse!”
And nineteen hundred people cheered.
Alma waited until they had gone around twice.
“You could say it again.”
“No.”
“He might — ”

“He knows.” Bahram was looking straight ahead over her shoulder at the far bleachers. “He knew before I said it. He has a map behind that stage with pins in it, he has been in ninety towns, he knows where Persia is. That is what I did not understand until just now.” He took the corner. “He is not making a mistake. There is no mistake to correct.”
He said it flatly and without any self-pity at all, and then he said:
“So. Barney.”
“I won’t call you that.”

“You will. Everyone will. It is shorter.” And after a moment, in a slightly different voice: “It is a small thing. I have had smaller things cost me more.” He took the corner. “And you are wearing one too. Everybody is. The difference is that mine is a costume and everyone can see it, and yours is invisible to you, and that is the whole of the difference, and it is enormous.”

The days had no shape. Forty-five on and fifteen off, and the fifteen went by like a hand passing over a candle, so the whole of your life became one continuous hour that kept starting over. There was no morning and no evening. The crowd was the only clock.

The food came on tin trays through a hatch in the wall and it came twelve times in every twenty-four hours, and it was the best food Alma had eaten in two years, and it was the thing that told her most clearly what kind of place she had walked into.

It was Chick Mullaly who explained why. Chick and Dot were the professionals — four contests that year, Wheeling and Louisville and two in Ohio, and they had arrived at the Rialto with their own shoes and their own foot powder and a way of moving that made everything Alma did look like an accident. Dot could sleep on her feet for eleven minutes at a stretch. Chick had a face like a closed shop.
“You know why it’s twelve, right?”
“Because they are generous,” Bahram said.

“Because you can’t quit on a full stomach.” Chick said it without any particular feeling, going past them on the outside. “Fella gets hungry, he starts thinking about his mother’s kitchen, and then he’s out the door in an hour. Every promoter knows that. It’s the cheapest thing they do. Best food I’ve had in two years, and I’ve had it in nine states, and every plate of it’s a nail.”
“How many of these have you done?” Alma said.

“Nine. Two we won.” He said it the way a man tells you his trade. “My old man saw the first ones, back east. College kids, twenty-three, twenty-four — see who can go the longest, get your picture in the paper, go home Sunday. Stunt.” He watched the floor going past. “Then the money went out of the world, and now there’s fellas running ’em in forty states, and you look around this room, kid. You see any college in here?”
Alma looked.
“No.”

“You want to know how it works, it’s three things and they’re all the same thing. He’s got to fill that bleacher every night for six weeks, and after the first Saturday there ain’t a soul alive pays a quarter twice to watch the same forty people walk. So: he starts running races, and the races break you. He starts finding out what’s wrong with each of you, and he sells it. And he’ll run a horse or two.”
“A what?”

“A horse. Fella that knows the racket, on the payroll, in the contest.” Chick steered Dot around the corner without waking her. “Keeps the floor from emptying out in ten days. Ferrin’s got ’em in every town. Nothing personal in it.”

Alma laughed, because it was two o’clock in the morning of the fourth day and it sounded like a thing that happened to other people, and she did not think about that conversation again for sixteen days.

They set their arrangement in the first week without ever discussing it. He took the outside of the circle, which was longer, and denied it when she said so. He talked and she didn’t — he had worked out by the third day that she would go somewhere behind her own eyes if the silence got long enough, and that she came back slower each time.

And they worked out the sleeping. Around the sixtieth hour you stopped being able to keep your eyes open on the floor, and the answer, which every single person in that building arrived at independently and none of them were taught, was that you slept standing up while your partner walked you. Ten seconds, thirty seconds, sometimes two or three minutes. Your legs kept going. That was the part Alma never got used to and never stopped thinking about afterward: that her legs kept going. She would come up out of it in a different corner of the room, with the music at a different place in the song, and her feet would have covered forty feet of maple without her.

“Your turn,” he’d say, and she’d put her head down on the wool of his shoulder. Then, later, “My turn,” and he’d put his down on her, and she’d take his weight, and he was heavier than he looked and got lighter every week.
Ida came around every four hours with a brown bottle with no label and poured it into a little tin cup, and there was a second bottle, a smaller one, that came out only at night.
“What is it,” Alma asked the first time.
“That one’ll keep you up. The other one’ll put you down.”
“But what is it?”
“It’s on the tray as Cordial,” Ida said. “That’s what the tray says and that’s what I call it, and hon, it’s four dollars a week and I don’t ask.”

It tasted like licorice and something underneath the licorice that was not licorice. Twenty minutes later Alma noticed that the cymbals had gotten louder, which she assumed meant the drummer had gotten louder, and it was three weeks before she understood that the drummer had had nothing to do with it.
Bahram took his and did not comment.
“You’ve had that before.”

“Something like it. There is a foundry job at the Rouge where you stand in front of an open door. The men who did that job were given something in their coffee in the summer of 1929, from a nurse, in a cup, and nobody asked what it was, and it tasted of licorice.” He shrugged with the shoulder she wasn’t using. “It is the same country. It is only a different room.”
The first hard night was hour seventy-something.

She stopped being able to feel her right foot from the arch forward — not numb exactly, it had become an object she was operating, a thing at the end of her leg that reported back late. She started to go down at the far corner by the fire door, and she knew she was going, and there was a long strange moment in which she watched herself go and had no opinion about it at all.
He caught her under both arms and got a knee behind her knee and walked her, and it took maybe eight seconds, and no judge saw it. When she came back up he was talking. He had not stopped talking.
“ — and the pier at Bandar, which is not a pier, it is four boards, and I stood on it with a bag and I was twenty-two years old and I had never in my life been out of sight of the mountain — ”
“Barney. I’m here.”
“I know,” he said. “I was talking so that you would have somewhere to come back to.”
“Thank you.”
“It is not a favor,” Bahram said. “If you go down, I go with you. You understand that this is the only reason anyone in this room is kind to anyone.”
“Is that true?”

He thought about it honestly. She would learn that he always thought about things honestly, that he was incapable of the small automatic lie that oiled every other conversation she’d ever had, and that this was going to be either the best or the worst thing about him.
“No,” he said at last. “But it is true enough to say out loud.”
II. THE HORSES
3. TABRIZ
She stopped talking on the eighty-eighth hour and did not start again for most of a day.
There was no reason. Nothing had happened. She had lain down on the cot and looked at the ceiling and something in her had simply put its tools down.

He tried a question. He tried a joke about the stew. He tried silence, and after about half an hour of it he did something she felt in her spine: he took his hand off her back for a second and put it down again lower and tighter, the way you’d take hold of something on a slope.

“I am going to talk now,” he said, “and you do not have to say anything at all. But I want you to listen, because if you go where you are going I will not be able to reach you and then we will both be walking out that door tonight.”
She said nothing.
“There was a man,” he said, “and he was the first man.”
The band was playing something with brushes on the snare.

“He lived in the mountains and he wore the skins of animals because nobody had made cloth yet. Nobody had made anything yet. He was the first, so everything that existed, he was the one who had to think of it. Fire. Cooking a thing before you eat it. He had a son, and he loved his son the way you love a thing when there is only one of it in the world, and something came out of the dark and killed the boy.”
Alma kept walking.

“And that is the first story,” Bahram said. “Not the making of the world. The world was already there. The first story is a father who has to go on being the first man after his son is dead, because there is nobody else to be it.”
They went around the corner by the fire door.
“What happened to him,” she said.
It came out of her like a splinter coming out.
“He wept for a year,” Bahram said, “and then he went to war, and he won, and it did not help. It is very old. Nobody had thought yet to say that it helped.”

She asked him where it came from and he said it was from a book, and she said what book, and he said the book, and she said what, and he looked at her with an expression she would learn to recognize as a man deciding whether to be insulted.

“It is a poem. It is called the Shahnameh. That means the Book of Kings, and that is exactly what is in it — kings, in order, from the first one to the last. It is sixty thousand lines. Everyone where I am from knows some of it and nobody has read all of it. It took one man thirty years to write.”
“Like the Arabian Nights.”
There was a pause of a length that she felt in her teeth.

“No,” Bahram said. “The Arabian Nights is a woman telling a king stories so that he will not cut her head off in the morning. It is a wonderful book. It is about stories. This is not that. This is what happened. Or — ” and he pulled himself back, visibly, “— it is what we say happened. It is the history of the world up until the part where the history gets written down by clerks and becomes boring.”
“You’re angry.”
“I am a little angry, and I would like to state that it is not with you, it is with a man in Ohio in 1926 who told me that where I come from is a place where people ride carpets.”
“Tell me the next one.”
“Not tonight. Because you have started listening,” Bahram said, “and that is worth more than a story. I am going to make it last.”

Her own education went the other way and she was, she would admit later, a slower student. She had thought Persia was near Egypt. She said so out loud on the fourteenth day and there was a silence of a quality she had not previously experienced.
“Egypt,” Bahram said.
“I don’t know! It’s — it’s all — ”
“Finish the sentence.”
“It’s all over there,” Alma said, “and I’m from Harlan County, Kentucky, and I’ve been to Detroit and once to Cincinnati, and I’m not going to apologize for it.”
And Bahram laughed. Properly, out loud, head back — the only time she heard him do it in the whole first thousand hours — and he laughed so long that a judge came over to see if something was wrong.

“That,” he said, when he could, “is the first honest thing anyone in this country has ever said to me about it. Two thousand miles from Egypt. Further than you are from Mexico.” He steered them past the stage. “And I want to be fair. I could not find Kentucky on a map in 1924. I thought all of America was flat.”
“It’s not flat.”
“I have since learned that it is not flat,” he said gravely.

And they arrived, over about a week, at the deal. She would call him Barney out on the floor, because everybody did, because the alternative was a small war every hour with a man on a microphone. Off the floor — in the fifteen, in the dark where nobody was selling anything — she would use his name.
She was bad at it for four days and then she had it.
“Say it again,” he said, the first time she got it clean.
She said it again.
“Once more, please.”
She said it a third time.
“Thank you,” Bahram said, and did not explain, and got up at the horn and went out and answered to Barney for nine hours.
He told her about the mountain in the small hours of the eighth day, when the bleachers were down to about sixty people and the band was three men.

“Tabriz is in the north. It is high. There is a mountain called Sahand and it is on your left when you go out of the city to the south and it is the first thing I ever saw and the last thing. Everything in my life until I was twenty-two happened where I could see that mountain.”
“What was your house like?”

“Small. Flat roof. In the summer we slept on the roof.” He walked her past the stage. “There was one of me, and there was my mother, and there was a very great deal of quiet. My father left in the winter of 1911. I was nine.”
He told it plainly, in the order it happened, without decorating it, and she understood by the fourth sentence that he had told it before and probably to himself.

There had been Americans in Persia. That was the part she couldn’t get her mind around. In 1911 the government in Tehran had been broke and badly governed and half-eaten by the Russians and the British, and somebody had had the idea of hiring an American to come and run the treasury — an actual American, from Washington — and he had come, with a staff, and Bahram’s father had been one of the Persian men who worked for them.
“He was a clerk. He wrote numbers in a book. He was very proud of it, and I remember that he began to wear a different collar.”
“What happened?”

“The Russians did not like it. They put soldiers on the road to Tehran and gave the government two days to send the Americans home, and the government sent them home.” He was quiet a moment. “That is the whole of it. Two days. A country decides something in two days and forty years happen to you because of it.”
“And your father went with them.”

“My father went with them. He said he would send for us. He said six months. He was not lying — I want to be accurate about this, because it took me twenty years to be accurate about it. He was not lying when he said it. He meant it in the room, out loud, with his hand on my head.”
The band went into the song for a couple going out, somewhere behind them, and the crowd sang.

“He wrote for two years. Then he wrote less. Then there was a war and everybody stopped writing. My mother kept the letters in a tin that had been a tin of English biscuits and she read them in an order that she had worked out and she never told me what the order was. She died in 1919 — there was famine in the north, and it was not one thing that killed her, it was the whole of that year. I was seventeen. I sold the house and I kept the tin.”
“So you came here to find him.”
“No,” Bahram said, too fast, and then, “yes. Of course. Yes.”
They went around.

“I told myself it was work. I told the man at the consulate it was work. I told myself for four years on the way — because it took four years, I went to Baku and I went to Constantinople and I was in Constantinople for nineteen months painting numbers on buses — and every single day of it I told myself I was going to America because America is where the work is.”
“And?”
“And that was also true,” he said. “That is the thing that nobody explains to you about a lie you tell yourself. It is not that it is false. It is that it is true and it is not the reason.”

Alma put her head down on his shoulder for a while. When she came up he was still walking, and the room had gone that particular green-brown color it went at four in the morning, and he said, as though there had been no gap:
“I chose my name on the boat.”
“You what?”

“My mother called me Abbas. It is a fine name. Half the men in the city are called it. On the boat there was a man from Rasht with a book, and I read it for eleven days, and there is a king in it called
Bahram who was a hunter, and when I came to the desk in New York and the man said name, I said Bahram.”
“You can’t just — ”
“You can. That is what America turns out to be.” He almost smiled. “You can do it once, at a desk, in eight seconds, and then it is done and there is nobody alive who can tell them otherwise.”

She thought about the ledger at the card table and a fountain pen and a line that said the undersigned certifies that all statements given upon entry are true, and she felt something go cold along her arms.
“Did you find him?” she said.
Bahram walked four or five steps.
“That,” he said, “is a different story and I am saving it.”
At six in the morning Ida was going down the row with the small bottle, and when she got to Alma she stopped.
“You been crying.”
“No.”
“Hon, I been doing this eleven years and I can tell in the dark.” She poured out the little tin cup. “Drink that. And listen to me. Whatever he’s telling you out there — ”
“He’s telling me stories.”

“I know what he’s doing,” Ida said. “I seen it before. It works.” She capped the bottle. “You just remember there’s a fella with a microphone forty feet from here whose whole business is finding out what a person’s got and selling it back to ’em, and the only two people in this building he don’t know a thing about is you and the Sheik.”
4. THE STORY SHE TELLS
She told him on the ninth night — the third of October, hour two hundred and sixteen — and it was the only time in eleven hundred hours that she started a conversation.
They were down to forty couples and the bleachers were maybe a third full because it was a Monday and it was raining.
“I want to tell you something,” Alma said, “and then I don’t want to talk about it again. I mean it. Not once.”

“Then you should not tell me,” Bahram said. “Because if you tell me I will want to talk about it, and I will have to spend the next month not doing it, and I am already carrying as much as I can carry.”
“I have to tell somebody.”
He walked her four or five steps.
“Then tell me,” he said. “And I will not bring it up. That is a real promise and you may hold me to it.”
“I’m from Kentucky. Harlan County. My daddy was in the mines and his daddy was in the mines and I got out at twenty-five, which where I’m from is not getting out, that’s running off.”
“Why did you run off?”

“Roy.” She said the name and it did nothing to her, which was interesting. “Roy Sutter. He came through with a road crew in ’27 and he had a way of standing that I liked and we were married in April and in Detroit by August, because they were paying five dollars a day at Ford’s and everybody in Harlan County had heard about it, and half of them came.”
“They were paying four in 1931,” Bahram said, “and then they were paying nobody. I was there for both ends of it.”
“Both ends.”

“In 1929 that one company had a hundred and twenty-eight thousand men. I know the number because it was painted on a board at the gate and I walked past it every morning for a year and I was proud of it.” He took the corner. “In the spring of this year it had thirty-seven thousand. That is not a business becoming smaller.
That is ninety thousand men going home in three years and every one of them going home on a particular afternoon, on his own, to a particular room.”
“Ruth came in May of ’28.”
That was the first time she’d said the name out loud since the summer and she had to walk a while before the next part.

“She was — ” and she found she had nothing. All the words for it were the same six words everybody used and none of them were the thing. “She had a way of holding a cup with both hands like it was heavy. Even when it wasn’t. Even at four. I don’t know where she got it.”
“Go on.”

“Roy was laid off in the spring of ’31 and then he got on again in the fall for eleven weeks and then that was it. He went out every morning for about a year.” She could hear the rain on the roof over the music. “He went to Toledo in February. He said there was something at Willys. He wrote once in March. There’s no letters after March.”
“You do not know if he is alive.”

“I don’t know if he’s alive.” She said it flatly. “And I’ll tell you the ugly part, which is that by June I’d stopped hoping he was, because if he was alive it meant he’d chosen, and I could carry the other thing better.”
Bahram made a small sound of understanding that had no words in it and she was grateful for it for the rest of her life.
“I was at the laundry on Vernor till May. Then they cut to two girls. And then it was just — ”
She stopped.
“You do not have to.”

“I’m going to.” She got her breath. “It was July. It was the eleventh of July, it was a Monday, and I carried her there myself. I want you to know that. Whatever else, I carried her there myself and I didn’t let anybody else do it.”
“Where?”

“Out past Northville,” Alma said. “It’s a long way. I had a nickel for the streetcar as far as it goes and then it’s a walk. It was ninety-some degrees. She had on the blue dress with the smocking, because that was the good one, and I did her hair, and I remember thinking it was a stupid thing to be doing, doing a child’s hair on a day like that, and I did it anyway and I took my time over it.”
She heard her own voice going and let it go.

“There was a woman there. She was kind about it. They were all kind about it, that’s — that’s a thing nobody tells you, that everybody’s kind and it doesn’t touch it at all. And there was a form to sign, because there’s always a form.”
“Yes.”

“And then I couldn’t stay.” Alma’s hands had closed on the back of his shirt. “That’s the part. I want to say it out loud one time. I couldn’t stay. I got up and I walked out of that building and down that road and I did not look back at it, not once, not one time, because I knew if I looked back I wasn’t going to be able to do it, and so I have never seen — ”
She stopped.
Bahram walked her around the corner by the fire door and past the bandstand and around again, and did not say anything, and did not ask her to finish the sentence.
“So that’s July,” she said, when she could. “And that’s why I’m in a dance hall in Ecorse, Michigan.”
He waited a long time before he spoke, long enough that the band changed songs.
“What is the money for?”
“What?”
“The thousand dollars. Everyone in this building has a number. Chick and Dot want a boarding house. The boy from Wyandotte wants a truck. What is yours?”
“Does it matter?”
“It matters more than anything else about you,” Bahram said. “It is the only thing in here that is real. Everything else is what we tell each other at four in the morning.”
The rain got harder on the roof.
“A stone,” Alma said.
“A stone.”
“A headstone.” She looked at the maple going by under them. “They’re eleven dollars for the small kind, with a name on it. And a date. I priced it.”
“Eleven dollars.”
“Eleven dollars.”
“And the prize is one thousand.”
“Yes.”

He did not say the obvious thing. She had braced for it all through the sentence — then why are you here, Alma, for eleven dollars, for a piece of rock — and he did not say it, and she looked up at him and his jaw was set and he was staring at the far bleachers.
“All right,” he said.
“That’s it? All right?”
“You said you did not want to talk about it again.” Bahram took the corner. “So. All right.”

He kept that promise. He never brought it up — not in the sixth week when she was hallucinating and would have told him anything, not at the end, not once in eleven hundred hours did he ask her a single question about the eleventh of July, and at the time she thought it was the finest thing anybody had ever done for her.
Thirty-nine years later, in a room in Dearborn with a photograph on the wall, she would still be trying to work out whether it had been.
5. HEEL AND TOE
The gate fell off in the second week and Doyle went to work.

The board said two hundred and forty on the fourth of October and there were forty couples left, and Alma had worked out by then that the contest she had entered and the show Doyle Ferrin was selling were two different things happening in the same room. The first Saturday there had been nineteen hundred people. The second Saturday there were maybe eleven hundred, and on the Tuesday after that she counted three hundred and stopped counting.
Doyle explained it to them himself, standing on the edge of the maple with the microphone down at his side, off, talking to the dancers like a foreman.

“You’re too good,” he said. “That’s the problem. Forty couples and every one of you looks like you could go another month. Nobody pays a quarter to watch forty healthy people take a walk.” He looked down the line. “So we’re going to start doing derbies. That’s a race. You’ll hate it. It’s how this works and I’d rather tell you than let you find out.”

The first one was a heel-and-toe. The toe of the back foot had to touch the heel of the front foot on every step, no gap, no running, and you went around the outside of the floor for one hour, and the last two couples to make each lap dropped out of the race, and the couple standing at the end got twenty dollars.
Doyle held it up in the air, four fives, and the room came alive for the first time in eight days.
“You do not have to win,” Bahram said, while they were lining up.
“Twenty dollars.”

“You do not have to win. Doyle needs a spectacle and a spectacle needs somebody to break in front of everybody. If you decide to win this you will be that person, and you will be that person in front of a photographer, and then he will own you.” He shifted his grip on her hand. “We finish in the middle. Every time. That is the whole plan and it is the plan for six weeks.”
“Twenty dollars is — ”
“Twenty dollars is two weeks of your life,” Bahram said. “Do the sum properly.”
She did the sum properly. She hated it.
They finished eleventh out of forty and Chick and Dot Mullaly won, and the crowd went home happy, and it cost her the skin on both heels.

The derbies came every day after that and they were all different and they were all the same. Figure-eights, twenty-five laps. Elimination sprints for the men while the women stood at the rail and watched. Something Doyle called a dynamite sprint, which was three minutes of actual fast dancing and was worse than an hour of anything else.
And they ruined the storytelling.

That was what Alma noticed first, and she was ashamed of noticing it. Not her feet. Not the twelve pounds she’d lost. The fact that from the tenth day onward, the hours that had been for talking got eaten, because a derby left you unable to put a sentence together for two hours afterward, and by then it was cot call.
“We are losing it,” she said, on the eleventh night.
“I know.”
“You said you’d make it last. There isn’t going to be — ”
“I know, Alma.” He rubbed at his eyes with the back of his wrist. “I have been thinking about it for four days.”
The answer came at hour two hundred and seventy and it came from Doyle, who did not know he had given it.

They were in the middle of a heel-and-toe, ninth lap, and Doyle was calling it over the microphone — look at the Sheik, folks, look at the footwork on that fella — and there was nothing at all to look at, Bahram was doing the same shuffle as everybody else, but Doyle said it and the crowd looked, and something went across Bahram’s face that Alma had not seen before.
That night he stopped in the middle of the floor.
“Give me your hands.”
“What?”
“Both hands. Face me.” He took them. They were still moving — you had to be — but he had turned her so they were square on, chest to chest, hands joined, sliding sideways. “Now. There was a king.”
“Barney, I can’t — I’m not going to remember a — ”

“You are not going to remember it,” he said. “You are going to learn it. There is a difference and your legs know it and your head does not.” He pushed her left hand out and up, and she went with it, and they turned. “There was a king. He had everything. He had ruled for three hundred years and he had made — ”
He turned her under his arm, badly, and she stumbled, and he caught her.

“Again. He had made everything. Cloth. Medicine. Ships. Bricks. Every good thing in the world, he had thought of it.” He turned her again and this time she came around clean. “And after three hundred years he stood up in front of everybody and said: all of this is mine. I made it. There is nobody above me.”
“What happened to him?”
“That turn,” Bahram said, “is what happened to him.”
She did it again. Out, under, around. The light went across her face and away.

“That is the whole story. That turn. When you do that turn you are Jamshid, and you are saying I did this myself, and everything he had came off him like a coat. His men left. His country left. He ran for a hundred years and they caught him in the end.” He stopped her. “Now. Show me.”
Alma did the turn.
“Again.”
She did it again.
“That is Jamshid,” Bahram said. “You have him now. You will have him in forty years. I could take the whole poem out of your head with a hammer and your arm would still know that.”

It became the method and it saved the book of it. He blocked it out in pieces small enough to survive a derby — a step, a turn, a lift of the elbow, a way of setting the shoulders — and each one was a piece of the story, and he’d give her one in the good hours and then, in the ruined hours after a sprint when neither of them could speak, he would just do it, put her through the figure, and she’d come out the other side with the story sitting in her without a word having been said.

“It is not mine,” he said, when she told him it was clever. “This is how it was always done. Nobody read that poem for eight hundred years. There was a man in a coffee house with a stick and he acted it out. He did the voices. He did the fighting. That is what it is for.”
“So I’m the coffee house.”

“You are the coffee house,” Bahram agreed. “It is not a large coffee house and it has one customer and the customer is on the floor of an automobile showroom in Michigan.” He turned her under his arm. “But it is running.”

By the eighth of October the board said three hundred and thirty-six and there were thirty-six couples, and Alma had lost nine pounds, and there was a man in the third row on the north side who came four nights a week and never brought anybody with him.

She noticed him because he was the only person in the building who did not eat. Everybody in those bleachers ate — peanuts, sandwiches out of paper, Doyle sold hot dogs at intermission for a nickel — and this man sat with his hands on his knees and watched the floor and left when the lights came up. He was maybe fifty. He wore a jacket that had been a good jacket. There was something wrong with his left hand; he kept it curled.
“That man was at the Rouge,” Bahram said.
“How can you possibly — ”
“Because of the hand, and because of the way he does not spend money.”
The story came on the thirteenth night and it came because of the man in the third row.

“After Jamshid there was a king who had a snake on each shoulder,” Bahram said, at half past one in the morning, squaring her up. “His name was Zahhak. A devil kissed him on both shoulders and two black snakes grew out of the places, and they could not be cut off — cut one and two grow — and they had to be fed. Brains. Two men a day. Every day. For a thousand years.”
Alma stopped laughing before she had properly started.

“And it works, that is the horrible part. He rules. He builds. There are roads. There are officials with ledgers, and a man in every town whose job it is to bring the two names, and the country gets used to it. That is what the poem is about. Not the snakes. The getting used to it.”
She looked out at the sixty or seventy people in the bleachers at half past one in the morning, and at the man in the third row with his hands on his knees.
“How does it end?”

“A blacksmith. His name was Kaveh and he was nobody — not a prince, no army, a man who made nails. He had eighteen sons and the snake king took seventeen of them, one at a time, over the years, and Kaveh said nothing, because what does a man who makes nails say.” He turned her under his arm. “And then they came for the eighteenth. So he went to the palace. And there was a paper there that all the great men of the country had signed, saying the king was a just king and that everyone was content, and they put it in front of Kaveh and told him to sign, because they wanted a workingman on it.” Bahram’s voice had not changed at all and that was somehow the worst of it. “And he read it. And he tore it up in front of the whole court. And they were so astonished that they gave him back his son and let them both walk out.”
“That’s not — ”

“It is not the end. He walked out into the street with his boy and he took off the leather apron he wore at the forge — the thing he wore to keep the sparks off, it was filthy, it was a rag — and he put it up on a spear. And that was the flag. That was the flag of the country for a thousand years afterward. Kings put jewels on it. It was carried into every battle in the poem. And it was a blacksmith’s dirty apron and everyone knew it was a blacksmith’s dirty apron and that was the entire point of it.”

He said the last of it a little louder than he needed to. Not much. Not so that anybody would have called it shouting. But the man in the third row had turned his head, and was watching them, and Alma understood with a small cold shock that Bahram had known he was there and had been telling it to him.
They went around twice more.
“March,” the man said.
His voice carried. There were sixty people in that room and no crowd noise to swallow it.
Bahram stopped them.
“March,” the man said again. “The seventh of March. Were you there.”
“No,” Bahram said. “I had been laid off fourteen months. I read it in the paper like everybody else.”

“I was there.” The man turned the curled hand over in his lap and looked at it. “Three thousand of us walked out to the Dearborn line to ask them for work. That’s all it was. Ask. And they had the fire hoses on us at the bridge and it was twenty degrees, and then they started shooting, and they killed four boys, and the oldest one of ’em was twenty-five.” Nobody in the bleachers moved. “They shot ’em in the back. And I’ve been out of work since the twenty-ninth of April and I come here four nights a week because I can’t stand to be in the house.”
Alma did not know what to do with her face.
Bahram let a moment go by. Then he said, evenly, across forty feet of empty maple:
“Then you already know the story. I have only been telling you the old version.”
The man looked at him for a long time.
“Fella,” he said, “what’s your actual name?”
And Bahram told him.

The man tried it. He got it wrong the first time and Bahram corrected him and he got it on the second, roughly, badly, but he got it — the first American mouth to hold it in eight years — and he nodded once and sat back and put his hands on his knees.
He was there on the Thursday and the Friday. On the Saturday he wasn’t, and he never came again, and Alma looked for him at the end and he was not in the room.
Doyle had been standing at the edge of the bandstand for the last of it with the microphone off. He came over at the horn.
“That was good,” he said.
Neither of them answered.

“No, I mean it. That was good.” He was not being sarcastic. That was the thing about him she could never get past — he was never sarcastic. “The snakes and the fella with the apron. Where’s that from?”
“It is a poem.”
“Huh.” Doyle nodded, thinking. “Could you do that up there?” He pointed at the microphone stand with his chin. “In front of the house. On a Saturday.”
“No.”
“Twenty dollars.”
“No,” Bahram said.
Doyle grinned at him with the whole of his face, entirely without malice, the way a man grins at a fish that has just gone off the hook and is still in the water and is not going anywhere.
“Okay,” he said. “Sure. Not tonight.”
III. SILVER SHOWER
6. THE BIRD
Ida changed the Cordial in the third week and did not mention it.

Alma knew because of the licorice. The licorice had always been on top of something and now the something had come up through it, a flat metal taste at the back of the tongue that stayed for an hour, and the warmth that used to come twenty minutes after arrived in four.
“This is different.”
“It’s the same bottle, hon.”
“Ida.”
Ida looked at her for a second and a half.

“It’s stronger,” she said. “There’s twenty-nine couples left and Ferrin wants eight by the end of the month and a person can’t do that on beef stew.” She capped it. “You want the old one, I’ll give you the old one, and you’ll be out by Friday.”
Alma drank it.

The sounds went first. That was the part nobody had warned her about and the part she could never afterward describe to anyone in a way that made sense. It was not that things got louder. It was that they stopped being sounds and started being touch. The cymbal became a thing that landed on the skin of her face. The air horn stopped being possible — she would stand in the last minute of the forty-five with her whole body braced against a thing that had not happened yet, and when it came it went through her like a hand pushing her chest, and twice she found she had put her arms up.
“It is the bottle,” Bahram said.
“It’s not the bottle.”
“Alma. It is the bottle.”
“Then why aren’t you — ”

“I am,” he said. “I have been for four days. The lights have edges on them. There is a green line around Doyle.” He turned her at the corner. “I did not tell you because I was hoping I was the only one, and if that seems stupid to you, I agree.”
The zombie treadmill was on the eighteenth day.

Doyle explained it to the crowd with real pleasure. The couples were blindfolded — actual cloth, tied around the eyes — and then bound together at the wrist with a leather strap, and then they raced. Twenty-five laps of the outside of the floor, blind, roped, at speed.
Alma stood at the rail while Ida tied the cloth and understood that she was frightened in a way she had not been since July.
“Don’t fight it,” Chick said, going past. “Fella that fights it goes into the bleachers. Just let your feet do it. Your feet know the room.”
The horn.
Here is what she could remember of it afterward, which was not much and was not in order.

The floor was longer than the room. She knew the room was ninety feet and the floor under her went on for a great deal more than ninety feet and there was no contradiction in it at all; it simply was.
The crowd was above her and also below her.
There was a bird.

It was in the roof. It was in the girders over the bandstand and its wings went out past the walls of the building on both sides and it was made of gold and blue in flat pieces like a window in a church, and it was not frightening. That was the thing she came back to for the next forty years. She had never in her life seen anything less frightening. She was blindfolded and roped to a man and running, and there was an enormous bird in the ceiling of an automobile showroom in Ecorse, Michigan, and she felt about it exactly the way you feel when somebody sits down next to your bed.
She was crying inside the blindfold before the tenth lap and she did not know it until it got to her chin.
They came thirteenth. Somebody went into the bleachers on the eighth lap and it was not them.
“There was a bird,” she said, in the parts department, with the cloth still in her hand.
Bahram was sitting on the edge of the men’s cot with his head down between his knees and it took him a long moment to lift it.
“What?”
“In the roof. A bird.” She was shaking. “Barney, I’m going out of my mind.”
“No.”
“There was a bird — ”
“Alma.” He got up and came around the end of the canvas, which was not allowed. “Listen to me. What did it look like.”
“Gold. And blue. Like — like a window.”
He sat down on the floor next to her cot with his back against the wall.
“All right,” he said. “Then I have to tell you about Zal, and I am going to do it now, out of order, and badly, because we have nine minutes.
“There was a baby born in the mountains, and his hair was white.”
“White.”

“Snow white, from the day he came out. His father was a great man and he looked at that child and he was ashamed of him. He thought it was a curse or a devil’s child or a punishment, and he could not bear that the country would see it.” Bahram had his eyes shut. “So he took the baby up onto a mountain and he left it on the rock. To die. Because it was easier than being looked at.”
Alma had gone very still.

“And there was a bird,” Bahram said. “She is called the Simorgh. She is old — she is older than everything, she has seen the world burn three times — and she nests on that mountain, and she came down to take the baby to feed her own young. And she picked him up. And she looked at him.”
“And?”

“And she did not eat him. She took him back up to the nest and she raised him. For years. She fed him and she taught him to speak and she kept him warm under her wing, and he grew up in a nest on a rock with birds, and he did not know he was a man.”
The horn was going to go in three minutes. She could feel it coming the way you feel a train.

“His father dreamed about him,” Bahram said, “years later, when he was old. And he went up the mountain, and he stood at the bottom of the rock and called, and the Simorgh looked at the boy — who was grown by then, a young man with white hair, who could speak the language of birds — and she said: there is your father. He has come for you. You may go.”
“Did he go?”

“He went.” Bahram opened his eyes. “That is the part nobody can ever explain. He went. She gave him a feather and she said, if you ever need me, burn this and I will come, and he walked down the mountain to the man who left him on it, and he never once, in the whole rest of the poem, said a word about it.”
Alma sat on a cot in a parts department with a blindfold in her fist.
“Why are you telling me this.”

“Because you saw her,” Bahram said, “and I did not want you to spend one hour thinking you were mad. You are not mad. You are a person who has not slept in eighteen days and something in you went and found the biggest thing I ever gave you and put it in the roof. And because the story is not about a bird. It is about a man who left a child on a rock because he could not bear to be looked at, and then lived to be old, and dreamed.”
She said nothing at all.
The horn went off, and went through her chest like a hand, and they got up and went out and walked.

It was the eleventh of October. The board said four hundred and eight and there were twenty-nine couples left of ninety-one, and they had been on that floor eighteen days, and there were twenty-nine to go and not one person in that building knew it.
7. THE HORSE
It happened at half past three in the morning on the twelfth of October and it took eleven seconds.

Alma had gone out at cot call to find Ida, and Ida was not in the parts department, and the light was on over the desk in the little office that used to be where they wrote up the finance on a Studebaker.
The door was open four inches.
Doyle was at the desk with the ledger. Bahram was standing in front of it.

Doyle counted bills off a roll — she could see his thumb doing it, three, four, five — and put them on the desk and turned them around, and Bahram picked them up and folded them once and put them in his trouser pocket.
Neither of them said anything. That was the part. There was no conversation. It was the eleven-second transaction of two men who had done it before and had nothing left to arrange.
Then Doyle said, “Same Friday,” and Bahram said, “Yes,” and Alma got herself back around the corner of the corridor before the door moved.

She lay on the cot for the rest of the fifteen with her eyes open and her heart going like a bird in a box, and she did the arithmetic, and the arithmetic came out clean the first time, which was how she knew she had been stupid for nineteen days.
A man who knew to slide his feet on the first night. A man told me at the door. He was very sure.
A man who knew, on day one, that the arch comes down. That you would want the cot in the light. That the fifteen minutes would start being stolen from you.
A man who had never done this before.

A man who said, on the very first night, in front of nineteen hundred people, not one word from that man is going to be true — and who was, at that moment, on the payroll of that man, and had been since before she walked in the door.

They had not been matched. She had stood in a line in a green dress and Doyle Ferrin had walked down the row of men and put his hand on one and moved on and stopped at the third, and she had thought that was chance, and it was staging. It was the oldest staging there was. Chick had told her about it himself in the second week and she had listened to it as a story about other people.
They’ll run a horse or two. Fella that knows the racket. Ferrin’s got ’em in every town.
The horn went off and she got up and walked out onto the maple and put her hand in his.
She did not say anything for eleven hours.

That is not a figure of speech. She counted them later off the board, because she wanted to know, and it was eleven hours and about twenty minutes, and in all that time she did not speak one word to him.
He knew inside of ten minutes. She felt him find out — a change in the hand on her back — and then she felt him decide not to ask.

So he talked. He talked the entire eleven hours, through four meals and a heel-and-toe derby and the whole grey hollow middle of a Wednesday morning when the bleachers were empty and the band was Fitz alone and the room smelled of the mop. And every time she went — every time her head came down on his shoulder and her eyes went — she came back up somewhere else on the floor with his voice still going, unbroken, in the middle of a sentence, holding the place.
He did not once ask her what was wrong.
At three in the afternoon on the twentieth day she said:
“I saw Doyle pay you.”
Bahram walked her four steps.
“Yes,” he said.
“That’s it?”
“You asked me a question that was not a question.” He took the corner. “Ask me the real one.”
“How long.”

“Since the second of September. Twenty-two days before it opened.” His voice had nothing in it. “He was hiring in a room over a hardware store on Fort Street and there were sixty men there, and he took four of us.”
“To do what.”

“To last.” Bahram said it simply. “That is the whole job. He needs a floor that does not empty out in ten days. So he pays men who know how to stand up, and they stand up, and it looks like a contest. Chick and Dot are on it. There is a man called Prescott on it who went out in the second week because Doyle told him to.”
Alma’s mouth was very dry.
“And me,” she said. “The pairing.”
“Yes.”
She had one more conversation about it, on the Thursday, and it was short.
“Are you going to stop?”
“Taking his money?” Bahram considered it. “No.”
“No?”

“If I give it back he replaces me,” he said. “There are three other men on that payroll and he does not need four. And if he replaces me, he replaces me tomorrow, and you are paired with a stranger at hour four hundred, and you will not survive that. Neither would I.” He turned them at the corner. “So no. I am going to keep taking five dollars a week from a man I dislike in order to remain the person holding you up. If there is a clean way to do that I have not found it in three days of looking.”
And that was the entire trouble with him, she thought, and it was going to be the trouble with him right to the end: he was never once wrong, and it never once helped.
She had not forgiven him. She wanted that on the record too.

On the Friday the judges made their selection and number sixty-three was on the list, and from that night the eight best took their fifteen minutes out on the maple in front of the house, under the spotlight, on the iron cots, where the people who had paid a quarter could watch them sleep.
Alma stood at the rail and heard her own number and felt her whole body come up off the floor with relief.

That was the thing she could not get over, standing there — that a man had bought her partner before she’d ever walked in the building, and had chosen her off a card in a ledger for reasons she still did not know, and had now decided to put her body on public display for fifteen minutes an hour — and her entire animal self had risen up in that moment and said thank God, I can lie down.

She went down onto the canvas and it did not matter at all that they were watching. She had thought, standing at the rail, that she would feel it. She felt nothing. Doyle worked the house — there she is, folks, that’s number sixty-three, she’s been on her feet since the twenty-fourth of September — and Alma Sutter lay on an iron cot in a green dress in a cone of white light and was asleep in under nine seconds.

The shame came later, and it was not about being looked at. It was that when the horn went, she had cried out. Out loud. In front of them. She heard herself do it as she came up, an animal noise of pure grief at being made to stand, and she got up and she saw a woman in the second row put her hand over her mouth, and Alma understood exactly what that woman had come for and exactly what she had just been given for twenty-five cents.
“You are going to want to tell me it is not so bad,” she said, later.

“I am not going to tell you that. It is worse than everything else in this building. The derbies only take your legs.” He walked her past the bandstand. “In the poem there is a thing that happens to kings. There is a light on them — every king has it, it is how you know he is the real one, it comes down on him and it sits on him like a — ” he made a small helpless gesture with the hand on her back “ — I do not have the word. A brightness. And when a king does the unforgivable thing, it goes out of him, and everyone can see it go, and after that he is just a man in a room.”
“And?”

“And that is the opposite,” Bahram said. “That is what I keep coming back to at four in the morning. It comes on you and it means you are finished. Doyle puts the light on the ones he has decided are ready to be watched coming apart.” He shook his head slightly. “It is the same light, Alma. It has only been turned around.”
Her arch came down on the fifteenth of October.

Not all at once, not with a sound, the way she had somehow expected — it had simply gone on going down, the way a roof goes down, over hours, and at some point in the small hours of that morning the thing that had been holding the middle of her foot up had stopped doing it, and now every step put the whole of her weight through a place that had never been built to take weight.
Ida knelt down at the four o’clock and looked, and did not put her thumbs in this time, and said, “Well.”
“Well what.”

“Well, it’s down. You keep the shoe on. Waking and sleeping, and I mean to the end, whatever end that is. You take it off and the swelling comes up and it don’t go back in.” She laced it tighter than Alma would have and tied it off. “And you shift it. You put more on the left. And in about four days the left one’s going to start, and then you shift it back, and that’s how it goes till the end.”
“Ida — ”
“Hon, I’d lie to you if I thought it’d help,” Ida said, and got up.

She did not tell him. She had promised Ida and she kept it, and it lasted about nine hours, which she thought later was a fairly good showing. He found out at the one o’clock in the morning because she went down at the corner by the fire door and this time it was not a lean, it was a drop, and he got both arms under her and it was closer to forty seconds, and a judge saw the whole thing and stood there with his hands behind his back and watched and did not call it, and Alma could never work out why.
“How long,” Bahram said, when she was upright.
“Since four.”
He said something in his own language, one word, short, and it was the only time in eleven hundred hours she ever heard him do it.
“Which foot.”
“Right.”
He steered her over to the outside line and put himself on her right side, and from that hour to the end of the contest he never once walked on her left again.

They found a way to do it inside a night. He took her weight on the turns — she would come round on the bad foot and there would be a hand under her elbow lifting about a third of her off the maple for the half-second it took, and it was so small that she doubted a judge four feet away could have named it.

And they invented, between them, in the small hours of the fifteenth of October, a thing they never gave a name to, in which he would say Jamshid and she would do the turn — out, under, around — because the turn came off the ball of the foot and not the arch, and it bought her three or four steps of relief, and by the end of that night she was doing it thirty times an hour.
“You are going to wear that story out,” he said.
“It’s the only one that doesn’t hurt.”
“Then it is the right one,” Bahram said. “You may have it. It was never mine anyway.”

Nothing else happened on the fifteenth of October. That was the truth of it and she went over it a great many times afterward, over years, looking for something in it, and there was nothing. The gate was four hundred at the matinée and six hundred at night. There was a figure-eight derby at seven and they came out fourteenth. A couple from Ypsilanti went out at ten past nine and Doyle wrote their verse on a cigarette paper on the corner of the bandstand:
I saw my mother in the second row,
I saw a bird as wide as Ohio,
I’d tell you the rest but I got to go —
So hold me up till the horn.

Alma heard it for the first time at half past ten on the night of the fifteenth of October, standing on a foot that had come down that morning, and she thought: he saw one too, then. And she looked for the man from Ypsilanti to ask him about the bird, and he had already gone out the door.

Sonny hung the five and the double naught that afternoon and Doyle made a small ceremony of it — a fanfare, and the four hundred people in the bleachers counting down out loud from ten while the boy went up the ladder, and then the twenty-four remaining couples in a line at the rail, still moving, always side to side, while he said their numbers and where they were from.
“Number sixty-three. Alma Sutter, Harlan County, Kentucky, by way of Beaufait Street. And her partner. Folks — the Sheik of Ecorse.”
The applause was warm. There were people in that room who had been there four nights a week for three weeks.
Alma smiled and raised a hand and did not hear any of it, because at that moment her entire being was concentrated on the middle of her right foot.
The cots came out at midnight. She was on them, in the light, and she slept eleven minutes.
8. SILVER SHOWER
Doyle came to her with it on the Tuesday, the eighteenth of October, alone, without the microphone.

“Twenty-two couples. Six hundred hours Wednesday. And I got two hundred people in that house on a weeknight and I’m paying a band.” He was leaning on the rail while she went past and he timed the sentences to her circuits, picking up where he’d left off each time she came round, which took a kind of skill she had to admire. “I want to run a silver shower Saturday. I put a couple up front. I hand ’em the mic. They tell the folks about themselves — where they’re from, what brung ’em here, the hard part. And the folks throw change on the floor. And whatever lands, they keep.”
Alma went around.
“How much does it land,” she said, when she came back.
“Eleven dollars is the ceiling. That was a wedding.” He straightened off the rail. “Think about it. I’ll ask the Sheik too but he’ll say no. He says no to everything and then he does it.”
Bahram said no.
“He’ll come back,” Alma said.

“He will come back on Friday and he will offer money,” Bahram agreed. “And I will say no on Friday as well, and then he will find another way, because a man like that does not go through a wall, he goes around it, and he has three weeks.”
“He said you’d say no and then do it.”
Bahram was quiet for a step or two.
“Did he,” he said.
She did it on the Saturday and she did not tell him beforehand.

That was deliberate. She sat with it through the whole of Friday and she worked out, quite coldly, that if she told him he would argue, and that he would be right, and that she would then have to either lose the argument or go against him having lost it, and both of those were more expensive than simply walking out onto the maple on a Saturday night and taking the microphone out of Doyle Ferrin’s hand.
Eight hundred people. Best gate in nine days.
“Number sixty-three,” Doyle said. “Alma Sutter.”

And he gave her the microphone and stepped back, and the band went quiet, and she stood in the middle of a maple floor moving side to side because a judge was watching, holding a live microphone, in front of eight hundred people, with her right arch flat and her hands shaking.

She had planned to tell them about Harlan County. That was what she had decided in the small hours — the mines and Roy and coming north for five dollars a day — and she opened her mouth to do it and what came out was:
“There was a boy.”
The room went very still.
She would think about that first sentence for the rest of her life — where it came from, why it came, whether some part of her had planned it and not told the rest. She was never able to decide.

“There was a boy,” she said, “and he was a king’s son, and he was the best of them. That’s not me talking. Everybody said it. He was straight and he was good and he was the only one in the whole family worth a damn.”
Somebody in the bleachers laughed at worth a damn and somebody else shushed them.

“And the king’s wife — she wasn’t his mother, his mother was gone — she took a shine to him. And when he wouldn’t have her, she went to the king and she said the boy had come after her. And she cried when she said it, and she was good at it, and the king believed her.”
She had them. She could feel it. It was the strangest sensation she had ever had, eight hundred people going quiet in a body.

“So they said, all right. There’s a way to settle this. And they built two fires.” Her voice did something on fires and she let it. “Two mountains of thorn wood, a hundred yards apart, and they lit them both, and they said: if you’re innocent, ride through. Ride between them. And if you’re telling the truth, God’ll bring you out the other side.”
“Did he do it?” a woman shouted.

“He did it,” Alma said. “He put on white. He got up on a black horse and he rode into the fire in white clothes in front of the whole country, and there was so much smoke nobody could see anything for a long time, and everybody stood there. And then he came out the other side. Not a mark on him. Not a mark on the horse. Not a hair of it burned.”
She let it sit the way she had watched Doyle let things sit for four weeks.

“And it didn’t matter,” Alma said. “That’s the thing I come to tell you. He proved it in front of God and everybody and it did not matter one bit. His father couldn’t look at him after. Couldn’t stand him in the house. Sent him off to a war on the other side of the world to be rid of the shame of what he’d nearly done to him.” She was crying now and she did not stop. “And they killed him out there. They cut his throat over a basin and they poured him out on the ground like he was nothing, and he was twenty-some years old, and he had never done one wrong thing in his life.

“And I want to tell you what happened where the blood went in. A plant come up. Out of the dirt. Right where it soaked in. It come up green and it kept coming up green and they couldn’t kill it and it’s growing there yet.”
She stopped.
