The first coin came down before she had the microphone away from her mouth.

Twenty-two dollars and forty cents. It took four men eleven minutes to sweep it and Ida counted it in a cigar box and Doyle stood over her while she did it and did not touch any of it, which Alma noticed.

“That’s a record,” Doyle said. He sounded genuinely delighted. “That’s a record for this outfit and I’ve been running it since ’29.” He looked at Alma and there was nothing in his face but professional pleasure. “Where’d you get all that?”
“I made it up.”
“Sure you did,” Doyle said, and laughed, and went to find the band.
Bahram was on the far side of the floor when she came back out and he had not moved for the whole of it. They walked half a circuit before either of them spoke.
“Siyavash,” he said.
“Yes.”
“You got the horse wrong. It was black, that is correct. You did not say his name.”
“I didn’t want to say his name.”
“No,” Bahram said. “I noticed that.”
They went around. The bleachers were emptying. Fitz was playing something slow.
“Say the thing,” Alma said.
“I am not going to say a thing.”
“Say it. You’ve been holding it for twenty minutes.”
He walked her past the bandstand.

“You told eight hundred people a story about a boy who was accused of something he did not do,” Bahram said, “and who proved it in front of everyone, and who was destroyed anyway. And they gave you twenty-two dollars.” He took the corner. “And I sat here and watched you and I could not work out whether you had chosen it or whether it had chosen you, and I have decided I do not want to know, and I am not going to ask, because I told you in the first week that I would not ask you anything.

“It is a beautiful story. It is one of the two or three most beautiful things in the poem and I gave it to you nine days ago and now it is worth twenty-two dollars and forty cents.” He was looking straight ahead. “I am not angry with you. I am trying to work out whether I am angry with myself for teaching you or with him for building the machine, and while I am working it out I would like to keep walking and not talk.”
So they kept walking and did not talk.
At the horn he said, without any preamble at all:

“Do it again next week. Twenty-two dollars is twenty-two dollars, and you will be off this floor sooner than either of us wants, and I would rather you left here with something in your hand.” He held the door for her, and stood back, and said, “After you.”
And she was too tired to argue about the door, and went through first, and that was the only time in eleven hundred hours it happened.
They built the seven over four nights in the last week of October and it was the only thing either of them ever made.

“There are seven,” he said. “There is a man called Rostam and he is the largest thing in the poem, and early on, when he is young, the king of the country is taken prisoner in a place full of devils and blinded, and Rostam has to go and get him. The road is seven days long and there is one thing on each day. Every child where I am from can count them off on their fingers.”
“So teach me the seven.”

“I am not going to teach you the seven. I am going to build you the seven, and at the end of it you will have seven things you can do with your feet when your feet are finished. That is not a story. That is a tool.”

The lion was a drop and a recovery, and it moved eleven pounds off the bad arch for the length of a bar. The desert with no water was a long slow sideways trail, four counts, the right foot only skimming the maple, and it was the best of them; she could do it for a full chorus. The dragon was a fast double turn on the balls of both feet and it was the only one that hurt, and she kept it because it woke her up. The witch was a dead stop — one count, both feet, and then away — and it was the only thing in four nights that was not motion and it was worth more than the rest together.

“That is the one people remember wrong,” Bahram said. “They think he saw through her. He did not see through her. He said a blessing over the wine out of habit and her face came off, and it was the habit that saved him.”

The man in the reeds had no step. Some of them are only a sentence, he said; leave it. The giant was a lift — an inch, maybe two, on the second beat of every bar, both her feet off the maple for half a second while he took all of her — and she was allowed it four times an hour and had to keep count herself, because he would give it to her every time she asked and then in a week he would not be able to walk.

And the seventh was the White Div, the devil in the cave, in the dark, where Rostam goes in blind and takes off its hand and then its head; and the blood was the point, because you had to carry the blood back and put it in the king’s eyes and that was what gave the man his sight again. The step for the seventh was the biggest thing they made: six counts, all the way around, a full circle with the man as the axis and her weight passed off her right foot three separate times inside it. It looked, from the bleachers, like the fanciest thing on the floor. It was pure engineering.

They ran the whole set for the first time on the thirty-first of October at about four in the morning and it took eleven minutes and nobody saw it. There were nine people in the bleachers. Fitz was alone at the piano.
“How long will it hold me?”

“A week,” Bahram said. “Perhaps ten days. Then your left will come down and we will have to build the whole thing again backward, and there will not be time.” He was breathing hard. “Do not ask me the next question.”
“I wasn’t going to.”
“You were.”
She was. She let it go.

Doyle put it in the show inside of three days, and by the first week of November there was a thing at the Rialto that the Free Press called the Persian dance, and eleven hundred people came out on a Saturday night in the fourth year of the Depression to see a woman in a green dress do it. Nobody in that building ever knew what any of it was. They did not know that the drop was a lion, or that the long trail across the floor was three days without water, or that the dead stop on both feet was a man saved by a habit he had not thought about. They knew it was pretty. They knew the girl with the bad foot did seven things in a row and that the last one went all the way around.
Ida changed the Cordial for the third time on the second of November and this time she said so.
“There’s fourteen couples and he wants six by Sunday.” She poured out the tin cup. “You can say no, and Chick and Dot will say yes, and Sunday you’ll be on Beaufait Street.”
Alma drank it.

It came on in ninety seconds and her jaw locked. Not clenched. Locked. She stood in the middle of the floor with her fingers on her own chin at eleven o’clock at night, in front of six hundred people, trying to work out whether she was going to be able to speak again.
Here is what she was able to say about the next nine hours, and she only ever said it once, in 1958, to a doctor who had asked her a different question.

The sound stopped being sound. A chord was not a noise, it was a shape that arrived at the skin and had corners on it, and when Fitz went up the keyboard she felt it go up her spine, note by note, like somebody walking two fingers. Every light had a rim. The pendant lamp over the middle of the floor had a green ring around it about a foot wide and the ring was not still. And she knew the horn was coming forty seconds before it came, every time, because the room got tight, and twice she screamed and could not hear herself do it, and after the second time Bahram put his hand flat over her sternum, which was not something he had ever done, and said, “You are in a building in Michigan and there are nine days left.”

At two in the morning the floor tilted about fifteen degrees toward the bandstand and stayed there. She danced on a hill for four hours, and found that her right foot was uphill, and thought quite clearly: this is the best thing that has happened to my foot in three weeks.

At three she watched a man in the second row take his face off and put it in his lap, casually, the way you’d take off a hat, and put it back on, and do it again. She watched him do it maybe fifteen times and felt nothing at all about it, and it was only days later that she understood the true horror of that hour was not the man — it was that being frightened would have required believing she was somewhere that things like that did not happen.
At half past three the bird came back. It came all the way across the roof, gold and blue, flat as a window, and settled with its wings out over the whole of the building.
“You came,” Alma said out loud.
“What?”
“Not you.”
Bahram looked up at the roof.
“Is she here?”
“She’s here.”
He was quiet for a moment. Then he said, “Good,” and kept walking, and Alma loved him for it in a way she was not able to examine for another thirty-nine years.
At seven Ida came down the row with the small bottle and Alma turned her face to the wall.
“It’s the down one, hon.”
“I don’t want it.”

“You want it. You don’t take the down one after the up one, you’ll lay there fifteen minutes with your eyes open and your heart going and you’ll come out worse than you went in.” She held out the cup. “Up one, down one, up one, down one. That’s the whole racket, and that’s why nobody who does one of these ever quite comes right afterward.”
Alma took it.
“And you pour it anyway.”
Ida capped the bottle and stood there a moment with her hand on the cot rail, an old woman with a bricklayer’s hands at seven in the morning in a room that used to be where they kept the carburetors.
“There’s a bottle in that tray for me too,” she said. “You want to see it?”
Alma did not answer.
“Get your fifteen,” Ida said.
It was three days before her hands were right, and she never again went a whole day without the rim on the lights.
9. THE PAPERWORK
Doyle sent Ida for her at ten past two in the afternoon on the fourth of November.
The office had a window onto the floor with a blind half down. Doyle was behind the desk with the ledger shut and his hands flat on top of it and there was a second chair, which there had never been.

He did not do anything for a moment. Then he opened the top drawer and took out a manila envelope with a string closure and unwound the string and laid three sheets of paper on the desk and turned them around.
She did not need to read them. She read them anyway, the way you touch a stove after you already know.
WAYNE COUNTY — SURRENDER OF CHILD FOR CARE — 11
JULY 1932. Her own signature at the bottom of the first page in a hand she did not recognize as hers, because her hand had been shaking. SUTTER, RUTH ANN. AGE 4 YR 2 MO. MOTHER:
SUTTER, ALMA. FATHER: SUTTER, ROY — WHEREABOUTS UNKNOWN.
And a second sheet, a carbon, stamped in October: STATUS —
RESIDENT.
“Sit back,” Doyle said. “You’ve gone grey.”
“When did you get these.”

“Fourteenth of October. I sent a fella.” He said it without any embarrassment at all. “I always send a fella. Every contest, every town — first two weeks I run down everybody that’s still standing. It’s not personal, sweetheart, it’s the business. I got twenty-two couples telling me twenty-two stories and I need to know which ones I can put on a handbill without some brother-in-law turning up with a lawyer.”
“You’ve had them three weeks and you never said.”
“No,” Doyle said. “I did not.”
Alma put her hands flat on her knees to stop them.
“Are you throwing me out?”
And Doyle Ferrin looked genuinely surprised, and then he laughed — not unkindly, he was never unkind, that was the thing she could never get past.

“Throwing you out? Honey, I got a woman on my floor who’s been on her feet nine hundred and eighty hours on a busted arch and does that Persian thing that put eleven hundred people in here Saturday, and you think I want you out?”
“I lied on the form.”
“Everybody lies on the form.”
“It says — ” her voice went “ — it says that all statements given upon entry are true.”

“It says that so I can throw you out if I want to throw you out,” Doyle said. “That’s the whole reason it’s on there. That’s what a form is.” He sat back. “I want to talk to you about the eighteenth. That’s where this ends — the hall’s let to a fella selling tractors after that. Fourteen couples. Election’s Tuesday and my gate is going to fall through the goddamn floor, because there ain’t a soul in Wayne County going to pay a quarter to watch you walk while there’s returns coming in.” He tapped the desk twice. “I want to bring her here.”
The room did something. She was aware of the blind, half down, and of the band starting up through the wall, and of a fly on the inside of the window.
“What?”
“I want to bring the little girl here,” Doyle said, “and put her in your arms in front of a full house.”
“No.”
“Hear it out.”
“No.”

“Alma.” He said her name the way he said things into the microphone, warm, unhurried, and it worked, it always worked. “You went out there Saturday and you told ’em about a boy that rode through a fire and they threw twenty-two dollars on my floor. Twenty-two dollars for a story you made up. This one’s true. This one’s a mother that put her baby in a county home in July because she couldn’t feed her, and danced six weeks to get her back. That ain’t a stunt. That’s the whole country. That is every single person in that bleacher and their sister.”
“You’d put her on a floor.”
“I’d put her in your arms.”
“For a quarter a head.”

“For a quarter a head,” Doyle agreed, “and you’d walk out of here with your daughter and eight or nine hundred dollars of silver, and I’d walk out with a full house on a Wednesday, and I don’t see the part where anybody’s hurt. That’s what I don’t see and I’ve been sitting on these three weeks looking for it.”
“Why?” Alma said. “Off the card. Number sixty-three. Out of ninety-one couples you had a man on the payroll and you gave him me — why?”
Doyle looked at her for a moment.

“Because you come in alone,” he said, “and you told me at that table that you had a little girl and that you had her in July, and you didn’t cry when you said it.” He shrugged, and it was the most honest thing she ever saw him do. “Sweetheart, a woman that don’t cry when she says that is a woman that’s got a long way left in her. I knew you’d go three weeks before you took your coat off.”
The horn went through the wall. Alma stood up. Her legs held, which surprised her.
“How long do I have to answer.”

“Sunday. And if you say no, we go on as we are, and you dance till the eighteenth and you take whatever you take, and I’ll shake your hand at the door and mean it.” He was already reaching for the ledger. “And you’ll be about two hundred short of the year at the county home, and they charge by the quarter, and they’ll have had her four months by Christmas.”
He said that last part while he was opening the book. Not as a threat. As a fact he happened to know, offered in passing, because he had sent a fella and the fella had been thorough.
Alma went out onto the floor and put her hand in Bahram’s and did not say one word about any of it for four days.
He asked Doyle for four hours on the Saturday morning and Doyle gave them to him.
She got hold of him at the twelve o’clock horn, in the corridor, with one hand in his shirt.
“Where are you going.”
“Out. I will be back at four.”
“Where, Bahram.”
He looked at her, and she watched him decide not to lie, and she watched him decide not to answer either, which was worse.

“I am going to be gone four hours,” he said, “and you are going to walk for four hours by yourself, and I am sorry about it, and it is the only thing I have asked this building for in six weeks. Do the seven. Do them in order and start again at the top and do not count the hours. Four hours is eleven rounds.”
“Tell me where you’re going.”
“No,” he said, and went.

Four hours alone on a maple floor. She had not been alone on it since the twenty-fourth of September, not for one minute of one hour, and she had not understood until that Saturday afternoon that the whole apparatus of her survival was a man’s body, and that without it she was a woman of twenty-nine with a collapsed arch walking in a circle in a room.
There was nothing to lean on. That was the first thing. She kept reaching.

There was nobody to talk. That was the second, and it was worse, and by the second hour she was talking out loud to herself in a low voice, saying the seven off on her fingers — lion, desert, dragon, witch, reeds, giant, div — and a judge came over at one point and put two fingers under her chin to check her eyes, and she said “I’m fine,” and he said, “I know. You’re saying things.”

There were maybe a hundred and fifty people in the bleachers, and after about ninety minutes of it Alma realised they had gone quiet. Not gone away. Quiet. A hundred and fifty people in a dim room watching a woman by herself, and nobody eating, and nobody talking.
Chick came past on the outside in the third hour with Dot asleep on his shoulder.
“You’re all right,” he said.
“I’m not all right.”
“You’re upright.” He steered Dot around the corner. “That’s the whole of it, kid. Everything else is decoration.”

Bahram came back at four minutes past four. She saw him come in the fire door at the far end and cross the floor toward her, and she was already going toward him, and he took her hands and put her straight back into the circle without breaking stride.
“Where were you.”
“Alma — ”
“Where were you.”
He walked her a full half circuit before he said anything.
“Do you remember that I told you I would not ask you anything?”
She stopped breathing.

“I have kept that. For six weeks. I have never once asked you a question about July and I am not going to start today and I am not going to answer one either. That is the same promise. It only looks different from this side.”
Here is what she noticed over the next thirty hours, and she noticed all of it and made nothing of any of it until Wednesday.

His coat. He had gone out in the brown coat he had come in with and he came back with it buttoned in a room that was seventy degrees and he did not take it off for the rest of the contest, not once, not on the floor, not at cot call, and when Ida told him to take it off he said no.
He stopped taking the Cordial. Ida came down the row and he shook his head, and she said, “You’ll go out,” and he said, “Yes,” and did not take it, and did not take it the next time either.

And he stopped telling her anything new — which was the one she should have seen, because it was the only thing in six weeks he had ever been reliable about. For thirty hours he did not start a single story. He talked constantly, about the band and the mop and the price of coffee in Constantinople in 1923, and there was not one king in any of it.
She asked him, on the Sunday morning, why he’d stopped.

“I have not stopped. There is one story left that matters and it is the largest one and I have been keeping it since the first week. I had thought I would give it to you at the end. I have changed my mind. I am going to give it to you tonight and tomorrow, because I do not think it should be the last thing.”
“Why not?”
“Because it takes two days to tell,” Bahram said, “and I do not know how many I have.”
That afternoon she went into the office and told Doyle Ferrin yes.

It took under a minute. Doyle did not gloat and did not smile and did not shake her hand. He wrote three words in the ledger and said, “Wednesday. Four o’clock, that’s hour eleven hundred, I’ll put it on the bills tomorrow,” and then he said something she thought about a great deal afterward.
“You want my advice?”
“No.”

“Tell the Sheik. Because I’ve run ninety of these, and the thing that busts a couple at the end ain’t the feet.” He shut the ledger. “It’s one of ’em carrying something the other one don’t know about. Every time. Ninety contests.”
“You’d know.”
“I would know,” Doyle agreed, entirely without irony, and reached for the telephone.
IV. THE GRIND
10. SOHRAB
Fourteen couples were left of ninety-one and there were three days to go, and on the Sunday night — the sixth of November, hour one thousand and thirty-two — he started the last story he had.
“There was a man, and he was the strongest man who ever lived, and he was the one I told you about at the horses.”
“Rostam.”

“Rostam.” He took her hands and squared her up the way he did when it was going to be a long one. “One day he went hunting on the border, alone, and he ate too much and he fell asleep under a tree, and while he was asleep some men stole his horse. So he walked. He was too proud to go home without it, so he walked into the enemy country — the one they had been fighting for two hundred years — and he came to a city, and he went in and said who he was.”
“And they didn’t kill him?”

“They gave him a feast. That is the part you have to understand about this poem or nothing in it makes sense. The king of the enemy country knew exactly who he was and put him at the head of the table, because you do not kill a guest, not even that guest, and because being able to say he had eaten in your house was worth more than his life.

“And that night the king’s daughter came to his room. Her name was Tahmineh, and she came in and stood there and told him the truth, which is that she had heard about him her entire life and had decided as a girl that if she ever had a child it would be his.” He steered them past the stage. “She did not flirt. She came in and said: I want a child from you and then you may go.”
“And he — ”
“He said yes. He sent for a priest that night and they were married before morning, because he was not a man who would do it otherwise. I want that in the record too.”
“How long did he stay?”
Bahram walked her three steps.

“One night. In the morning he took off his arm-band — a clasp he wore, and everybody in the world knew that band — and he gave it to her and said: if it is a girl, put this in her hair. If it is a boy, put it on his arm. And they found his horse the next day and he left. And he went home, and he did not send for her, and he did not go back, and in nine months she had a son and she called him Sohrab, and she put the band on his arm.”
“Did she write to him?”

“She wrote. He sent money, and gifts, and word that he was pleased. He was not a monster. He was a man with a country to defend on the other side of a war and a child in the enemy’s house, and he did what men do, which is that he meant to go, every year, and then it was another year.”
Alma had her head down on his shoulder.
“So the boy grew up without him.”

“The boy grew up enormous.” And there was, for one moment, something almost like joy in his voice. “He is his father’s son in every particular. At ten he could beat any man in the city. At twelve nobody would fight him. And he had never once been told who his father was, because his mother was frightened.”
“Of what?”
“That Rostam would send for him. That she would lose him. And that her own father would kill the boy if he found out whose he was. Both. Every day, both.”
“Did he ask?”

“He asked constantly. From the time he could speak. Who am I. Why am I bigger than everybody. Where is my father. And she told him nothing for fourteen years, and then one day he came and stood in front of her and would not leave, and she told him.”
“And what did he do?”
Bahram walked her right around the outside of the floor before he answered.
“He raised an army.”
“To fight him?”

“To find him.” He said it with a force she had not heard from him in six weeks. “That is the whole tragedy and everybody misses it. He did not go to fight his father. He went to war against his father’s country in order to locate his father. Because he was seventeen and enormous and he had been told a name, and the only thing he could think of that would bring a man like that out of a place like that was an invasion.”
“That’s insane.”

“He was seventeen. You are trying to solve the largest problem of your life with the only tool you have, and the only tool he had was that he was the strongest boy on earth. And it very nearly worked. He would break the border. Rostam would be sent for, because Rostam was always sent for. They would meet. And he would say: I am your son. And then — this is in the poem, he says it out loud to his mother before he goes — then the two of them together would be so strong that they could put whoever they liked on both thrones and there would never be a war again.”
“Oh God.”
“Yes.”
“Barney — ”
“That is where I am stopping.”
“You can’t stop there.”
“Tomorrow.” He was walking her toward the gap in the bleachers because the horn was forty seconds out; she could feel it coming through the floor. “I told you it takes two days.”
“Just tell me whether the boy finds him.”
Bahram stopped at the gap and looked down at her for what was probably two seconds, and there was something on his face she had never seen there and did not see again until Wednesday afternoon.
“He finds him,” he said.
The horn went off.
He told the rest on the Monday night and he told it badly.

That was the thing she came back to. Six weeks of a man who put a sentence down like a full cup, and on the seventh of November 1932, from about eleven at night until nearly four in the morning, he told her the largest story he had and he could not do it. He stopped in the middle. He went back and did pieces again. Twice he lost the thread entirely and stood there with his mouth working and she had to say the tent, you were at the tent, and he said, “Yes. The tent.”
She thought it was the Cordial coming out of him. He had not taken it in three days.

“They met on the field. There is a fortress on the border and the boy took it in an afternoon, and the king sent for Rostam, and Rostam came — late, drunk, four days late, because he had been sent for a hundred times and it had never once mattered.”
“Did he know who he was fighting?”
“Nobody knew. The boy was seventeen and no one had heard of him. He was simply the largest man anybody had seen since Rostam.”
“Did the boy know?”

“The boy suspected the whole time. That is the first thing. Sohrab looks across at this man and something goes through him and he asks. He asks him directly, in front of both armies. He says: I think you are Rostam.”
Alma had stopped walking properly and he corrected her with his knee.
“And?”
“And Rostam said no.”
“He lied?”

“He said, I am not Rostam. I am a servant of Rostam’s.” Bahram’s voice had gone flat. “And there is a reason for it and it is a good reason and it is the worst thing in the poem. He is old. He is the most famous man alive. And a boy he has never heard of has just taken a fortress in an afternoon, and Rostam looks at him and thinks: if this is the one who finally beats me, then let it be a nobody who beats a nobody. Let there not be a song about the day Rostam went down.”
“He lied about his own name to save his reputation.”
“He lied about his own name because he could not bear to be seen losing. Yes. And every single thing that comes after is that one sentence.

“They fought three days. The first day they broke every weapon they had, and the horses gave out and neither of them could stand and they agreed to come back in the morning. And that night the boy went back to his own tent and said to his people — I am quoting it — he said: he is like me. When I look at him something turns over in me. I think this is my father.”
“And they told him no.”

“They told him no. A man in his own camp who knew the truth and had been sent along by the king specifically to prevent this, and he said: no, boy, I have seen Rostam and that is not him. And Sohrab believed him. Because he was seventeen and he wanted to be told what to do.”
“On the second day — ”
“On the second day the boy won.”
Alma looked up.

“He threw him. The strongest man who ever lived, on his back in the dirt in front of two armies, and Sohrab had a knife out and was on his chest. Seventeen years old. And Rostam said — ” he stopped. “He said: it is not our custom. It is our custom to let a man up the first time and take his head the second. And it is not true. There is no such custom. He made it up on the ground with a knife over him.”
“And the boy let him up.”
“The boy let him up.”
They went around the corner by the fire door. There were four people in the bleachers.
“Why?”
“Because he was decent. Because he was seventeen and decent and he wanted to be the kind of man his father would have been proud of, and he had no idea he was doing it in front of him.”
“The third day.”
“The third day he killed him.”
Bahram said it and kept walking and Alma had to make herself keep her feet going.

“They wrestled from morning. And Rostam got a grip, got him over, and had the knife in him before the boy hit the ground, and it was fast, and it was over. And then the boy said a thing while he was dying.” He walked four steps. “He said: this is my own fault and nobody else’s. I came here to find my father and I have been asking for him all my life and now I am dying in a strange country and I never saw his face. And then he said: do not think you are safe. My father will hear of this. Whatever hole you go into, he will find you.”
“Oh God.”
“And Rostam laughed. He laughed. And to be kind to a dying boy he asked: who is your father, then? Tell me his name.
“And the boy said the name.
“And Rostam went down on the ground.”
The band had stopped. Fitz had gone. There was a phonograph playing at the back of the hall on a low table, hissing more than playing.

“He tore the shirt off him,” Bahram said, “looking for the arm-band. And it was there. On his arm. Exactly where his mother had put it seventeen years before, exactly where he had told her to put it, the day he left.”
Alma was crying. She had not decided to.

“He tried everything. The king has a medicine that heals anything, and Rostam sent a man begging for it, and the king would not send it — because if the boy lived, the two of them together would be stronger than any throne on earth, and the king knew it.” He turned her under his arm, slowly, the Jamshid turn, the one that cost her nothing. “And Rostam sat there holding him and the boy died before the man got back, and he would have died anyway, because the king was never going to send it.”
“That’s the end?”
“He burned his own tents and cut his horse’s tail and went home and lived another two hundred years, and there is not one line in the rest of it about him being happy.”
They walked in silence for a long time.
“Why did you keep that one for last?”
Bahram did not answer.
“Barney.”
“Because it is the best one.”
“That’s not why.”
“No.”
She waited a full circuit of the floor, and past the bandstand, and around again.
“Ask me the question you want to ask,” he said at last, “and I will answer it, and it is the only one you will get.”

Alma thought about it for a long time. She had it. She had it right there — who are you in that story — and she stood on a collapsed arch at four in the morning on the eighth of November 1932 with a man’s arms around her and she was so tired that her mind put its hand on the wrong thing.
“Did Rostam ever tell anybody?” she said. “Afterward. Did he ever tell them what he’d done?”
Bahram walked her all the way around.
“No,” he said. “He said the boy was a stranger.”

And Alma said, “That’s the saddest thing I ever heard,” and put her head down on his shoulder, and went out for about ninety seconds, and came back up in a different corner of the room with his voice still going and no memory at all of what he had been saying while she was under.
11. TWO BITS AT THE DOOR
The handbills came off a press in River Rouge on the Monday afternoon and by Tuesday morning they were in every window in three towns.
WEDNESDAY 4 P.M. — HOUR 1100
SHE BURIED HER BABY IN JULY
AND SHE WANTS HER BACK
SEE IT HAPPEN ON THE FLOOR
25¢ — DOYLE FERRIN PRESENTS
Ida brought one in and put it on the cot without a word and went out again.
Alma read it four times.

Buried. He had left it in. She had told him the truth in that office with the blind half down, she had sat in a chair while he laid her own signature on the desk in front of her, and he had gone out and printed buried on eight hundred handbills, and it took her a full minute to work out why.
Because surrendered did not sell.

Because a woman whose child died was a woman the crowd could weep for, and a woman who had signed her daughter over to the county in July because she could not feed her was a woman the crowd would have to decide about, and Doyle Ferrin had never in ninety contests given a crowd anything to decide.
“Take it back.”
“Can’t. They’re up.”
“Then print another one.”

“Sweetheart.” Doyle had his coat on; he was going somewhere. “I got two hundred bills in windows from here to Wyandotte and a man in Toledo owed money and it’s Tuesday. What do you want me to do, go around with a bucket of paste?”
“It says buried.”
“It says something people’ll pay for.”
“It’s a lie.”

Doyle stopped in the doorway and turned around and for the first time in six weeks he looked at her with something other than professional warmth, and what was underneath it was not cruelty either, and that was the part she could never afterward explain to anybody.
It was patience.
“Alma,” he said, “you told me that at the table. On the twenty-fourth of September.” He put his hat on. “I wrote down what you said. All I ever did was print it.”
She did not tell Bahram.
She had four separate opportunities in the day that followed and she took none of them and she knew exactly what she was doing every time.

He would have seen a bill. That was the thing she kept in front of herself, the way you keep a hand in front of a candle. Everybody had seen one. They were in the window of the diner on the corner and in the drugstore and pasted to the fire door of the Rialto itself.
So he knew. He must know. And he had not said one word about it in twenty hours, and she told herself that meant he was letting her keep it, the way he had let her keep everything else.
That was the arithmetic she did on the eighth of November 1932 and it was the worst arithmetic she ever did in her life.

The verse went up on the Tuesday. Doyle wrote it on the corner of the bandstand in pencil the way he wrote all of them and handed it down to Fitz, and Fitz looked at it for a second and then looked up at Doyle, and Doyle said, “Play it,” and Fitz played it.
The Persian prince and the girl in black,
She buried her baby and she wants her back,
Two bits at the door — come see her get it back.
So hold me up till the horn.
There were three hundred people in the hall and about a third of them already knew the tune, because the tune was six weeks old and had been in every kitchen in Ecorse since the middle of October.
By the second time through, they were singing it.

Alma Sutter danced in a circle on a maple floor with a man’s arms around her while three hundred people sang a song about her dead daughter, who was not dead, and she looked at the floor going by under her feet and thought, with a clarity she never had again about anything:
I did this. Nobody did this to me. I signed the paper in July and I lied at the table in September and I said yes on Sunday, and everything since has just been machinery.
She got through it. She did the seven. Lion, desert, dragon, witch, reeds, giant, div, and back to the top.

Bahram did not say anything about the verse. He did something else. On the fourth time through, when the whole hall had it and the drummer had come in behind it, he stopped them dead in the middle of the floor — both feet, one count, the witch, the only still thing in the seven — and he put his hand flat on the back of her head and held it there against his shoulder so that she was facing into his shirt and not into the room.
He held it there for the whole verse. Eleven seconds, maybe twelve.
A judge started over and thought better of it.
And when the band went into the next thing he took his hand away and put it back on her waist and walked her on and said, in an ordinary voice, as though continuing a conversation about nothing:

“There were nine hundred people here on Saturday and there will be twelve hundred tomorrow and none of them will be able to tell you one true thing about either of us. That is not a small thing to have. Most people do not get it. Keep hold of it.”
Alma said, “Barney — ”
“I know,” he said.
She had not said anything yet.
“I know,” he said again. “It is all right.”
And she believed, for the next nineteen hours, that he was telling her he had seen the handbill and forgiven her for it.

The radio came on at eight on the Tuesday night and by ten it was over. Roosevelt had forty-two states before it was finished, and the hundred and ten people in that hall made a sound at Michigan that was not quite a cheer — it was lower than a cheer, it went on longer — and a man near the fire door put both hands over his face and sat down.

Alma Sutter, twenty-nine years old, who had not read a newspaper since the twenty-fourth of September and had no address to be registered at and had not voted, was in the middle of a maple floor being carried by a Persian who could not vote at all. The last event Doyle Ferrin ever ran at the Rialto was called the Argonne Forest, and the rule was that the men carried the women; every twenty minutes a judge blew a whistle and any man who had put his partner down since the last whistle was out. It was named for the battle because Doyle had a poster.
“Are you glad?” she said.
Bahram shifted her weight.

“I do not know what it means. I have been here eight years. In 1928 they said everything would change and it changed into this.” He walked eleven or twelve steps. “There is a thing at the end of the poem. After six hundred years of kings, the Arabs come over the border and it is finished, all of it, the whole world of the book, and the poet writes a letter from a general on the losing side to his brother, and the general says: I see what is coming and there is nothing to be done, and men who have nothing will be raised up, and men who have everything will be brought down, and the world will be turned over.” He shifted her again. “It is not a hopeful letter and it is not a despairing one. It is a man saying: it is going to be different and I will not be able to tell you whether it was better, because I will be dead.”
“That’s not an answer.”

“No,” Bahram agreed. “I am glad. I am glad because a hundred and ten people in this room made that noise when they said Michigan, and I have not heard anybody in this country make that noise in four years.”

Chick Mullaly carried Dot for three hours and twenty minutes without setting her down once, and at the end of it he was walking like a man in water, and Dot was asleep with her face in his neck, and Alma watched them go by and thought about a boarding house that was never going to exist.
Bahram carried her for the whole of it. He was thirty years old and he had lost twenty-two pounds since September and he had not taken the Cordial in five days.
She said, once, around two in the morning: “Put me down.”
“No.”
“Barney, they’ll let you set me down and pick me up, that’s not the rule — ”
“I know the rule. I am not going to put you down,” Bahram said, “because I am not going to be able to pick you up again, and I would rather not find that out tonight in front of these people.”
At twenty past three Doyle called it and there were seven couples left, and he stood on the bandstand under one work lamp and did the arithmetic in public.

“Hour eleven hundred is this afternoon at four o’clock, and that’s the finish. Whatever’s standing at four o’clock splits the thousand.” He rubbed his face. “But I ain’t splitting it seven ways. So we’ll grind in the morning. Six o’clock, straight through, till there’s four left.” He put the microphone down on the piano. “Go on. Get your fifteen. There’s nobody left to watch you.”
The grind started at six in the morning and Doyle announced the rules himself, on the floor, without the microphone.

“Seven couples and I need four by four o’clock. No rest. No fifteens. Horn’s off. You’ll eat on the floor and you’ll stay on the floor till there’s four. And no helping. That’s the part you’ll hate. No pinching, no pins, no slapping, no shaking, and — ” he paused “ — no talking.”
Somebody said, “What?”

“No talking. Not to your partner, not to anybody. Judges’ll call it. I know what you’ve been doing out there for six weeks and it’s the only reason half of you are still standing, and today it stops.”
Alma turned and looked at Bahram and Bahram was already looking at the ceiling.

“He is not stupid,” he said. It was the last thing either of them said out loud for nine hours. “He has been watching us since the twelfth day and he has finally worked out what the thing is that keeps you up.”
Then a judge came past and put a finger up and that was that.
The first hour was fine. The second was fine. By the fourth she understood what had been taken and it was not conversation.

It was that for six weeks she had been going under a hundred times a day — ten seconds, forty seconds, two minutes — and every single time she had come back up into the middle of a sentence. There had always been a voice already running. She had never once, in six weeks, surfaced into silence.

Now she surfaced into a room with fifty people in it and a phonograph and the sound of six other couples’ shoes on maple, and there was nothing to come back to, and each time it got harder to want to.

By the sixth hour she was going under and staying under and being walked, and she knew it was happening and could not do anything about it, and somewhere far off she could hear herself making a small noise on the exhale, over and over, like a hinge.
And then he started to dance it.
She never afterward knew what hour it was. Late morning. The light through the soaped windows had gone white.
She came up out of one of the long ones and her feet were doing something and she did not know what and then she did.
Out, under, around.
Jamshid. The king who stood up in front of everybody and said I made all of this myself, and lost it, and ran for a hundred years.

He was not saying it. His mouth was shut. He was putting her through the figure with his hands, and her body was going where it had gone thirty times an hour for three weeks, and the story came up in her without one word being spoken.

He gave her the lion. She dropped and he took it and gave it back. He gave her the desert — the long slow sideways trail, four counts — and she thought about a man following a ram because a ram must be going somewhere. He gave her the witch. Dead stop, both feet, one count. A man saved by a habit he had not thought about.

And then he took her right around, six counts, all the way, her weight coming off the bad foot three separate times inside the circle, and she came out of it upright and awake with her eyes streaming and a judge four feet away who had seen absolutely nothing at all.
She looked up at him. He looked back at her and did not move his face in any way whatsoever.
He kept it up for five hours. All seven, in order, over and over, in silence, on the last morning of it, in a room where talking had been made against the rules.
Doyle called it at one in the afternoon and by then there were four couples. He got up on the bandstand and said, “That’s four,” and turned the horn back on, and the whole floor made a noise.
Fifteen minutes.
They lay down in the parts department and Alma looked at the ceiling boards and could not make her hands stop.
Through the canvas, on the men’s side, Bahram said the first words he had said in nine hours.
“Alma.”
“Yes.”

“That was the last one. There is nothing left in the book that you do not have. I have been going through it for four days. There are eight hundred kings I have not told you about and there is not one of them that is any use to you.” She heard him turn over. “You have all of it. You have everything I brought.”
She lay in the dark with her hands going.
“Barney,” she said. “This afternoon at four — ”
“I know about this afternoon.”
“You’ve seen the bill.”
There was a pause that she took, at the time, for exhaustion.
“Yes,” Bahram said.
12. THE SPOTLIGHT

They started coming in at one in the afternoon, three hours early, and by half past two the Rialto was as full as it had ever been. Doyle put the number at fourteen hundred to the Free Press and Ida said afterward it was nearer sixteen, and that people were standing three deep behind the north rail, and that a man from the fire department had come and looked at it and gone away again.
They had come out on a Wednesday afternoon, the day after the election, in the fourth year of the worst thing that had ever happened to any of them.
There was a photographer. He came at two with a Speed Graphic and a case of flashbulbs and set up on a chair at the edge of the maple, and Doyle showed him where to stand.

She did not see the girl arrive. She had been on the floor since four in the morning, and the stage door was around behind the bandstand at the far end, and she did not see it and she never once, for the rest of her life, stopped being grateful for that.
Ida saw it. Chick Mullaly saw it and said nothing to anybody for eleven years and then said it to a man in a bar in Sandusky in 1943, which was how it got out at all.

Doyle had sent a man out to Northville on the Monday to fetch the child, the way he had sent a man out in October to find the papers, and the man had come back on the Monday evening and gone into the office and shut the door. Ida did not hear what was said in there. What she knew was that the bills stayed up in every window in three towns, and that on the Tuesday Doyle spent an hour on the telephone, and that on the Wednesday a different woman altogether came to the stage door.

She came at twenty past two with a little girl of about four in a coat too big for her. Doyle came out and talked to the woman for two or three minutes and gave her something, and Ida, who was standing eleven feet away with a tray of bottles, saw that it was a dollar bill and heard Doyle say that there’d be a plate for the both of them after and that they should wait in the parts department and keep the coat on her, because the coat was fine, the coat was good, leave the coat.
The girl had brown hair. That was all Ida could ever tell her. Brown hair, and she was small for four, and she was very good about waiting.
Bahram had been walking her in slow circles since noon and had said almost nothing all day.
At three o’clock he said: “What time.”
“Four.”
“And what will you do afterward.”
“Take the room back. Beaufait Street. It’s eleven dollars a month and the woman’s still got it. I’ll have her home by Thursday.” She was so tired that everything came out flat. “What’ll you do?”
“West,” he said.
“West where?”

“I do not know. West.” He turned them at the corner. “There is nothing here. There has never been anything here. There is a man in Chicago who is my father and there is a job at a plant that will not exist in three years and there is a room on Fort Street with my bag in it. Two hundred and fifty dollars will take a man a very long way west.”
Alma stopped.
“Say that again.”
“There is a man in Chicago who is my father,” Bahram said.
The crowd was singing. The band was six men again; Doyle had hired the other two back for the afternoon.
“You found him.”
“You found him and you never — ” Her mind would not do it. “Barney, you’ve had six weeks — ”
“I know.”
“What did he say?”

And Bahram Nasseri, thirty years old, of Tabriz and Constantinople and the River Rouge, looked out over the heads of sixteen hundred people in a converted automobile showroom in Ecorse, Michigan, forty minutes before the end of it, and said:
“He said, can I help you?”
She waited.

“That is all,” he said. “That is the entire story and I have been carrying it since the third night and there is nothing else in it. I stood in a shop on Halsted Street with rugs on the walls and a man came out from the back who was sixty-one years old and had my hands, and he said can I help you, in English, and I said no.”
“You said no?”

“I said no, thank you. I said I was looking for a different address.” Bahram was walking her again; she had not noticed him start. “And he said, what address, and he was kind about it — he was very kind, he came out from behind the counter to look at the paper I did not have — and I said the name of a street I made up, and he said he did not know it, and I said thank you, and I went out, and there is a bell on that door and I heard it ring behind me.”
“Why?”
“That is the question.”
“Why?”
He walked her a long way. Past the bandstand and the fire door and around.

“Because he did not know me,” Bahram said, “and if I had told him, he would have had to decide something. And he was sixty-one and he had a shop. And I stood on Halsted Street in the cold for about two hours afterward working out what I had done, and what I worked out is this — ” and here his voice went, for the only time in six weeks, and he took it back inside four seconds “ — I did not do it for him. I have said for three years that I did it for him. I did it because as long as I did not say it, he had not chosen. Do you understand? The moment I say I am your son, he has to choose, and then I will know. And I have been able to go on not knowing for three years and it has been the only comfortable thing in my life.

“That is Sohrab,” Bahram said. “You asked me on Monday who I was in that story and you asked me the wrong question because you were tired, and I let you, and I should not have. I am not the man who kills the boy. I am the boy who stands in front of him and does not say the name.”
Alma was crying.
The band stopped. Doyle Ferrin came out onto the maple with the microphone and the house came up on its feet, all sixteen hundred of them, and the photographer put a bulb in.
“Folks,” Doyle said. “Hour eleven hundred.”
Bahram took both her hands.
“Alma. Look at me.”
She looked at him.

“Whatever happens in the next four minutes,” he said, “I want you to know that I have never once lied to you in this building. Not one time. There are things I have not said. There is not one thing I have said that was not true.”
“Barney, what — ”
“Say my name.”
“What?”
“Please,” he said. “Say it properly. Once.”
And she said it.
He shut his eyes for about a second.
“Thank you,” he said. “That is the second time in eight years.”
And then Sonny came up the ladder at the back of the stage, and took down the numerals, and hung up eleven hundred, and the crowd started to count.
Doyle took his time, because he was good at his trade and it was the last four minutes of it he would ever do in that town.
He walked the four couples out to the middle and lined them up and had the crowd give each of them a hand. He held up the thousand dollars in an envelope and let sixteen hundred people look at it.
Then he said, “Now. Before we finish.”
And the hall went quiet, because they had all seen the bills, and they knew what was coming, and they had paid a quarter for it.
“There’s a girl on this floor,” Doyle said, “come in here on the twenty-fourth of September with a coat buttoned up to here and sixty cents in it.”
Alma stood in the light with her hands at her sides.

“Number sixty-three. Alma Sutter. And I’ll tell you what she told me at that table, because she told it to me straight and she didn’t cry when she said it, and I have thought about that woman every day for six weeks.”
The photographer had come out onto the maple.
“She lost her little girl in July,” Doyle said. “Four years old.”
Somewhere in the bleachers a woman said, “Oh, no,” out loud.

“And she come in here and she danced eleven hundred hours on a broke foot.” Doyle let it sit, exactly as long as it needed. “Well, folks. I got something to tell you and it ain’t in the papers and it ain’t on the bill outside, and I want you to hear it from me.”
He turned around.
“Bring her out,” he said.
The stage door opened at the far end past the bandstand and Ida Teller came out onto the maple holding the hand of a little girl in a coat too big for her.
Sixteen hundred people made a sound Alma had never heard before and never heard again.
She did not move.

That was the thing. She stood in the cone of the spotlight in a green dress on a floor she had been on for forty-six days and she did not move one inch, because the room had tilted again, fifteen degrees, and there was a rim of green light around everything, and there was a bird in the girders with its wings out over the whole building, and she had known since the middle of October that none of that was real.
So she stood there and waited to find out.

The girl came across the floor. She came slowly, because it is a very long way for a four-year-old, and because Ida was walking slowly, and because she had been told to. She had brown hair. She was small. She was holding the front of her coat with one hand the way a child does when the coat is too big.
And Alma Sutter went down on her knees on the maple in front of sixteen hundred people, which was a disqualification, and no judge in that building moved a muscle, and she put her arms out.
The flashbulb went off.

That was the photograph. It ran on the front page of the Detroit Free Press on the tenth of November 1932 under the headline A MOTHER’S ELEVEN HUNDRED HOURS, and it was reprinted in nineteen papers that month, and it was in a book about the Depression in 1970 and in a documentary film in 1979, and it is the only image of any of it that survives.
A woman on her knees in a spotlight in a torn green dress with the number 63 on her back.
A small girl in a coat, half-turned, one hand in the coat front.
The woman’s face.
Here is what Alma could remember, and she remembered all of it, every hour of the rest of her life, in perfect order, at any time she wanted it and a great many times when she did not.
The coat smelled of somebody else’s house.
The girl’s hair was finer than Ruth’s and there was more of it.
The girl said, “Are you the lady?”
And Alma said, “Yes.”

And the girl put both arms around her neck, because she had been told to do that, because a man had given her mother a dollar and said there’d be a plate for the both of them after, and because she was four years old and a woman was on her knees in front of her crying, and a child will hold anything that is crying.
Alma held her.

She held her for eleven seconds and she did not know. She was six weeks without sleep, on a bottle that made the floor tilt, in a cone of white light, in front of sixteen hundred people who were on their feet and weeping, and she held a child she had not seen since the eleventh of July, and she did not know.

And then the silver started. It came down out of the bleachers all around them, hundreds of coins, a noise like hail on a tin roof, rolling and ringing on the maple in the dark beyond the light, and the band was playing, and sixteen hundred people were singing the only three words in the American tongue.
Bahram was eleven feet away with a death certificate in the pocket of a coat he had not taken off in four days.
He had four seconds.

Alma did not see him make the decision because she was on her knees with her face in a stranger’s daughter’s hair. Nobody saw it. There is no witness to the four seconds and there never was one, and every single thing that happened afterward — the rest of her life, and his, and the letter and the package and the room in Dearborn — comes out of four seconds that nobody in that building was looking at.
What she heard was the crowd change.
That was all. A sound of sixteen hundred people going ah — a different ah, the wrong one — and she came up out of the child’s hair and turned around.
He was already down.
He had gone over onto his right side with his right arm out and his left hand up near his chest, and his knees were drawn up, and his head had gone back.
She knew that shape.

She had seen it a hundred times since Monday night — in the rafters, in the green rim around the lights, on the tilted floor at four in the morning: a boy on the ground in a strange country with a knife in him, telling a stranger that his father would come.

She was the only person in a hall of sixteen hundred people who knew what she was looking at, and she knew it because of a story he had told her on a Monday night, and she got to him on her hands and knees across a floor covered in coins.
“Barney — ”
He was breathing. His eyes were open.
“Barney, get up, you have to — ” she had his shirt in both hands “ — it’s four o’clock, it’s four o’clock, we made it, you have to get up — ”
And Bahram Nasseri looked up at her from the maple floor of the Rialto with the whole weight of a spotlight on both of them and said:
“No.”
“What?”
“Alma.” His hand came up and closed around her wrist. “It is done. It is finished. You are off the floor and nobody can say you stepped off it.”
She did not understand. She did not understand for a very long time.
“They’ll disqualify us — ”
“Yes.”
“You dropped — ”
“Yes,” he said.

And then a judge blew a whistle, and Doyle Ferrin said something into the microphone that she did not hear, and men came out onto the floor, and somebody took the little girl’s hand and led her away toward the stage door in the confusion, and Alma Sutter never saw that child again and did not learn her name.
CODA
13. ELEVEN HUNDRED HOURS

Doyle Ferrin split the thousand dollars four ways and paid it in cash at the door on the evening of the ninth of November 1932, disqualification or no disqualification, and told the Free Press he’d done it, and it was the last decent thing he ever did in that town and it cost him nothing at all.
Two hundred and fifty dollars.

Alma took it because she had two hundred and fifty dollars’ worth of reasons to take it, and because a woman came out of the bleachers and put a further forty-one dollars and sixty cents in her hands in a cigar box, swept up off the maple.
She went out to Northville on the Thursday morning, the tenth of November, on the streetcar as far as it goes and then the walk.
There was a woman at a desk who was kind about it. They were all kind about it.

Ruth Ann Sutter died on the fifteenth of October 1932 of diphtheria at the Wayne County home, at four years and five months, and the notification had gone out by post on the seventeenth to the last address on the file, which was a rooming house on Beaufait Street that her mother had given up on the twenty-third of September.
The letter came back. It sat in a dead-letter box in the post office on Fort Street, eleven blocks from the Rialto, for the whole of the contest.

She had danced through the night it happened. She had been asleep under a spotlight on an iron cot, on the fifteenth of October, at midnight, and Sonny had hung the five and the double naught that afternoon and Doyle had made a small ceremony of it and the crowd had counted down from ten.
She had felt nothing.

That was the part. There was nothing to find, and she looked for the rest of her life. She went over that day a thousand times — the eggs at two in the morning, a couple from Ypsilanti going out at ten past nine and a man who had seen a bird — and there was nothing in it, and there was never going to be anything in it, and the world had simply gone on being a room with a band in it.
She went to the Rialto on the Friday and it was a hall let to a man selling tractors.

Ferrin Amusement Co. had loaded out on the Thursday afternoon for Fort Wayne. Ida had gone with them, because Ida always went with them, and she left an address that turned out to be a boarding house that had never heard of her.
Alma asked a man where the Persian had gone and he said which one.
The rest of it went like this.

She took the room on Beaufait Street back and lived in it for nine years. She never bought a stone, because there is no stone on a county plot and she was told that plainly by a man at a desk who was kind about it, and she never asked a second time.

She got work at the laundry on Vernor in March of 1934 and stayed there until it shut in 1949. She stood at a press for fifteen years on a foot that had come down on the fifteenth of October 1932 and a second one that came down in 1935, and after 1938 she used a stick, and after 1955 she used two.
She did not marry again. Roy Sutter was declared dead in absentia in 1946 at her request and she never found out one thing about what happened to him and stopped wanting to somewhere around 1940.
She was on the front page of the Free Press on the tenth of November 1932 and people recognised her on the streetcar for about five months and then they stopped.
She had the green rim on the lights for the rest of her life.

And she did the seven. Every day, or near enough, holding the edge of a sink or the back of a chair — lion, desert, dragon, witch, reeds, giant, div — and she never told one living soul what any of them were, and there was nobody left alive who could have told them.
The package came in March of 1943.
Brown paper, string, no letter. Posted from Bakersfield, California, in a hand she knew immediately and had not seen since a cigarette paper on the corner of a bandstand.
Inside was a book.

It was old and it had been rebound badly and it was in a script she could not read, right to left, in a language she did not have one word of. There were pictures in it — flat, gold and blue, no perspective, men on horses with faces like moons — and she sat on the edge of a bed on Beaufait Street with it open on her knees and understood after about a minute what she was holding, and put her hand flat on the page.
Two places were marked with folded paper.
The first was a picture of an enormous bird carrying a white-haired child up a mountain.

The second was near the end. It had no picture. There was a folded sheet in it, and the folded sheet was a certified copy, stamped, of a death certificate issued by the County of Wayne, State of Michigan, for SUTTER, RUTH ANN, and it was dated the fifteenth of October 1932, and it had been applied for and paid for at a county office out past Northville on Saturday the fifth of November 1932 at twenty past two in the afternoon.
He had had it in his coat.

He had had it in his coat for four days. He had had it in his coat on the eighth of November while three hundred people sang a song about her dead daughter and he put his hand flat on the back of her head so that she was facing into his shirt. He had had it in his coat at four o’clock on the ninth of November while she went down on her knees in a spotlight, eleven feet away, with four seconds to decide.
There was no letter. There was never a letter.

She wrote to Bakersfield in April. The envelope came back in June marked NOT KNOWN AT THIS ADDRESS, and she wrote again in 1944 to the same address anyway, and that one came back too, and she did not write a third time.
She never told anybody.

That is the fact and it does not have anything underneath it. She had the certificate and the book from March of 1943 until she died and she never showed either of them to another human being, and there was nobody to show them to, because Ruth Ann Sutter had been dead for eleven years and had been dead for two of the six weeks in which sixteen hundred people wept for her mother.
She kept the photograph.

She had it framed in 1951, badly, at a place on Michigan Avenue, and she hung it in the kitchen of a two-room apartment in Dearborn where it stayed for twenty years: a woman on her knees in a torn green dress in a cone of white light, and a small girl in a coat too big for her, half-turned, one hand holding the coat front.
People asked about it. Everybody who ever came into that kitchen asked about it, because it is an extraordinary photograph.
And Alma Sutter would say: that was in the paper. That was a dance marathon in Ecorse in 1932. I was in it for six weeks.
And they would say, is that your little girl?
And she would say yes.
She was seventy-one. She had two sticks and an apartment on the second floor and a woman from the county who came Tuesdays.

There was a girl doing a project. She was nineteen or twenty and she was from the university at Ann Arbor and somebody had given her the name, and she came out to Dearborn in October with a tape recorder in a case and sat at the kitchen table and asked about the marathons.
She was very earnest. She had done her reading. She knew about the derbies and the silver showers and she had a photocopy of a handbill.
“They say people went out of their minds,” the girl said. “Is that true? Did you hallucinate?”
“I saw a bird,” Alma said.
The girl wrote it down.

They talked for about an hour. The girl asked about the food and the cots and the money and whether it was rigged, and Alma told her yes, it was rigged, they always had a couple on the payroll, everybody knew.
And then the girl looked past her at the wall.
“Is that the famous one?”
“That’s it.”
“God.” The girl got up and went over to it. “This is — I’ve seen this. This is you.”
“That’s me.”
The girl looked at it for a long moment, the way people did.
“And that’s your daughter,” she said.

The refrigerator was going. Outside a car went past. It was a Tuesday in October in Dearborn, Michigan, and there was one bare bulb over the sink with a rim of green light standing an inch off it, not quite still, the way there had been since 1932.
Alma Sutter put both hands on the table.

She had thirty-nine years of it. She had a book she could not read on a shelf in the other room with two folded papers in it, and a foot that had come down on the fifteenth of October, and seven figures she could still do holding the edge of a sink, and four seconds that nobody had been looking at.
And she had never once been able to decide.

That was the whole of it, in the end, and she had gone at it from every side for thirty-nine years — whether he had given her the last good hour of her life or taken the only one that was hers, whether a man who will not say a name is merciful or only frightened, whether she would have chosen it, whether anyone had ever asked her.

She had asked herself the question in 1943 and in 1951 and at three o’clock in the morning more times than she could count, and the answer had never come, and she understood by now that it was not going to.
“Yes,” she said. “That’s my daughter.”
And the girl turned off the tape recorder and thanked her and went back to Ann Arbor, and Alma Sutter sat in her kitchen and looked at a photograph on a wall of a child whose name she never learned.

In the poem there is a king who is the last good one, and when it is finished — when he has done everything he came to do and there is nothing left that anyone needs him for — he calls the men who love him and tells them to go home, and they will not go, and so he walks out into the mountains in the snow. They follow him. They follow him all day.
And there is a night, and in the night the snow comes, and in the morning there are no tracks at all, and the men stand there in the white looking at the place where he was.
The poem does not say that he died. It is very careful. It says only that he was not found.

GLOSSARY
Bahram [bah-RAAM] — The Persian dancer paired with Alma
Sutter, renamed Barney by the announcer on the first night; a king in the Shahnameh who was a hunter, and the name he chose for himself at a desk in New York.
div [DEEV] — Persian, demon. One of the monstrous beings of
Persian myth; the White Div is the seventh and last of Rostam’s
Seven Trials.
Jamshid [jam-SHEED] — The great early king who thought of every useful thing in the world — cloth, medicine, ships, bricks
— then stood up and claimed the credit, and lost all of it. The first step Bahram teaches: out, under, around.

Kaveh [KAA-veh] — The blacksmith who refused to sign the tyrant’s declaration that the country was content, tore it up in open court, and raised his filthy leather work apron on a spear as the flag of the rebellion.
Rostam [ro-STAM] — The greatest hero of the Shahnameh, whose
Seven Trials Bahram builds into dance steps, and who kills his own son in single combat without knowing him.
Sahand [saa-HAND] — The mountain south of Tabriz, visible from the city; the first thing Bahram ever saw and the last.
Shahnameh [shah-nah-MEH] — Persian, the book of kings.
Ferdowsi’s thousand-year-old epic of the Persian kings and heroes — as Bahram puts it, a book full of people who do not recognise each other until it is too late.

Simorgh [see-MORGH] — Persian, thirty birds. The ancient bird of the mountain, older than everything and witness to the world burning three times, who takes the abandoned child Zal and raises him in her nest.

Siyavash [see-yaa-VASH] — The blameless prince, falsely accused by his stepmother, who rode through fire to prove his innocence and was destroyed anyway. The story Alma sells from the microphone for twenty-two dollars and forty cents.
Sohrab [so-RAAB] — Rostam’s son, raised in the enemy country, who raised an army in order to find his father and was killed by him, neither of them knowing the other.
Tabriz [ta-BREEZ] — City in the north-west of Persia; Bahram’s home.
Tahmineh [tah-mee-NEH] — The princess who came to Rostam’s room in the night, married him before morning, and raised their son alone.
Zahhak [za-HAAK] — The king with a black snake growing from each shoulder, fed two men a day for a thousand years, whom the country got used to.
Zal [ZAAL] — The white-haired child left on a mountain by a father ashamed of him, raised by the Simorgh, and afterwards
Rostam’s father.
